The recent merge of JDK12 code to the extensions repository has caused the JDK12 builds to fail.
This seems to be related to Oracle moving some files from `src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal/misc` to `src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal/access`. The files that seem to have caused the OpenJ9 jcl source build to fail are: JavaLangRefAccess.java
SharedSecrets.java
as the package locations have changed and hence the import statements in the OpenJ9 jcl code that references these classes is incorrect and causes issues:

 ^

"find" takes a set comma separated parameters with no spaces

issue_title: Build all java executables with -pagezero_size on MAC
description:
-pagezero_size <hex> can be used for both compressedrefs and non-compressedrefs variants. This will allow executables to work with both compressedrefs and non-compressedrefs OpenJ9 librarires.
If I use compressedrefs shared libraries in a non-compressedrefs SDK, then the executables such as java, javap ... would fail with `JVMJ9VM015W Initialization error for library j9gc29(2): Failed to instantiate compressed references metadata; 200M requested.`
Second, this change will provide a generic front-end where executables such as java, javap ... can be used with both compressedrefs and non-compressedrefs shared libraries.
This change also is one less thing to do in the future when compressed / default jvm sidecars are merged.
- [x] jdk8 - [x] jdk11 - [x] jdk.next ibmruntimes/openj9-openjdk-jdk#51

issue_title: Cannot wrap Object.notify() with a JVMTI agent
description:
With a JVMTI agent, it's generally possible to replace or wrap native methods using the NativeMethodBind event. When running on OpenJ9, I can't seem to do so for java.lang.Object.notify().
The NativeMethodBind even is invoked whenever a native method is bound to a class. My expectation is that the agent gets a notification for all native method of all loaded classes. However, I don't seem to be getting an event for Object.notify().
The sample project in demonstrates the issue - when running with HotSpot/OpenJDK, both Object.notify() and "my" method are detected. When running on OpenJ9/OpenJDK, only "my" method is detected.
My end goal would be to wrap Object.notify() one way or another, in order to detect when it is invoked.
Thanks,
Uri.

issue_title: Investigate possible native stack space optimizations
description:
The interpreter entrypoints (like sendClinit, etc) all take 5 arguments, which is a leftover from the builder days when those calls created the interpreter stack frame. This is certainly no longer necessary.
Also worth looking at is the 32-slot reserved outgoing argument area on various architectures. The interpreter no longer needs this (JNI calls are performed using libffi which builds its own stack frames as required).

issue_title: Image files are not displayed properly on SwingSet2 demo program
description:
Hello.
I used OpenJDK JDK11 + OpenJ9 for Linux amd64.
When I executed SwingSet2 demo, GIF images were not displayed properly.
And the situation was random, 4 GIF images were displayed on JInternalFrame Demo.
2 or 3 images were broken.
Version Information: RHEL 7.5
$ ~/OpenJ9/jdk-11.0.1+13/bin/java -version
openjdk version "11.0.1" 2018-10-16
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.1+13)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.11.0, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20181115_18 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 090ff9dcd
OMR - ea548a66
JCL - d4455071ce based on jdk-11.0.1+13)

1. Run following command
$ ~/OpenJ9/jdk-11.0.1+13/bin/java -jar ~/OpenJ9/jdk-11.0.1+13/demo/jfc/SwingSet2/SwingSet2.jar
2. Check Frame 0 - 4 windows. some of images are not displayed properly
This issue only happens on Linux amd64.
Linux ppc64le and s390x builds were OK.
It worked fine on following AdoptOpenJDK build.
$ ~/Hotspot/jdk-11.0.1+13/bin/java -version
openjdk version "11.0.1" 2018-10-16
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.1+13)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.1+13, mixed mode)
It seemed GIF image treated as interlace GIF.
But I checked interlace flag on GIF.
$ identify -verbose resources/images/misc/duke.gif | grep Interlace:
 Interlace: None
I checked the latest IBM Java8 for Linux amd64, but I could not recreate this issue.
I assume IBM Java8 applied a fix against class library on GIF image decoder related code.
But it seems register or memory area was not clean up properly.

issue_title: Simplify support of new Java versions
description:
The work leading up to and including eliminated the various complexities of managing several redirector variants: we should apply the same thinking to the JVM and JCL shared libraries. As the VM is built, `JAVA_SPEC_VERSION` identifies the version requirements.
Removing the extra JVM variants should be relatively straight-forward: we can use UMA directives:
<group name="jdk11">
 <include-if condition="spec.java11"/>
</group>
or cmake conditionals:
if(JAVA_SPEC_VERSION GREATER_EQUAL 11)
 # additions for Java 11+
endif()
to the description of a single JVM to account for version differences.
Similar changes address most of the issues for a single JCL, but the tool that generates the various `j9vmconstantpool_*.c` files will need to be changed to ease introduction of new versions. I propose to replace `jcl` xml attributes such as <classref name="java/lang/LayerInstantiationException" jcl="se9,se10,se11,se12" flags="opt_module"/>
with
<classref name="java/lang/LayerInstantiationException" versions="9-" flags="opt_module"/>
which will not need to be modified to add support for Java 13, for example. (The `opt_module` flag may even be redundant.)
When running `VMCPTool.Main`, the `-jcls se7_basic,se9_before_b165,se9,se10,se11,se12` option is replaced by `-version $(VERSION_MAJOR)` to specify the desired content of `j9vmconstantpool.c` (only one C file is generated - the one suitable for the JVM being built).

issue_title: Improved reporting in JMX MemoryPool MBean
description:
The JMX MemoryPool MBean should return the value of the max storage limits for the JIT Data Cache, Code Cache. These values default to 128 or 256M and can be set using -Xcodecachetotal.
 Without this data users are not able to understand if they have sufficient (or too much) storage allocated for the JIT, and have to be aware of what the default maximum sizes are set as. In addition if the storage areas are exhausted then the data from the MBeans can not be used to determine this.
**Proposed Solution**
Return the max size of the JIT data cache and code cache areas using the max value for the following MBean attributes (note currently this value returns -1)
a) java.lang->MemoryPool->JIT code cache->Attributes->Usage
b) java.lang->MemoryPool->JIT data cache->Attributes->Usage

issue_title: Add PR build capability for ValueTypes
description:
# Description
 - Add a PR build to test a ValueTypes enabled JDK. The valueTypes changes are not enabled by default and require to be compiled with specific flags turned on. For this reason, it cannot be tested with the existing PR builds.
# Reason for issue
- Valhalla is a multi-release project that contains many features. Some of these have already been released such as nestmates and varhandles. Some of these features are still to come, such as value types and specialized generics. In order to make progress on the upcoming features we need to prototype it in openj9. There is a risk if we commit changes without testing them so it is essential that we have a build that can run ValueTypes tests.

issue_title: Metronome GC - pause times increase with uptime
description:
Hello!
I noticed strange behavior when OpenJ9 is running when application is running as a daemon.
![image](
As you can see, 'GC quantum time maximum' usually is at 5 msec when the application is just started, increasing to 8-10 msec after ~40 hours of runtime (this varies and can be in the range 20-50 hours), but after ~105 hours it increases to 20 msec. I was unable to identify any relations between workload and pause times, but on another server I had an increase to 70-80 msec.
See attached verbose GC log and TGC rootscantime log.
[gc_tgc.zip](
OS version: Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.15.0-38-lowlatency
JVM version (I also experience same problem with 0.9.0 and 0.11.0):
openjdk version "1.8.0_202" OpenJDK Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_202-b08) Eclipse OpenJ9 VM (build openj9-0.12.1, JRE 1.8.0 Linux amd64-64-Bit 20190205_196 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 90dd8cb40
OMR - d2f4534b
JCL - d002501a90 based on jdk8u202-b08) This was briefly discussed with @amicic before.

issue_title: Implement jstack: display runtime state of a Java process
description:
Suggested command syntax:
`jstack <option>* <pid>*`
`<pid>*` is a list of target process IDs; if none are supplied, the PID(s) are read from `stdin`. A user may then query all processes via `jps -q | jstack`. IDs of dead processes are silently ignored.
By default, `jstack` prints the Java stacks and thread information of the specified processes: this essentially the information in `java.lang.management.ThreadInfo`.
Options:
- `-p`: also print the process's system and agent properties
- `l`: also print information about ownable synchronizers.
- The usual suspects: `-J`, `-h`.
`jstack`'s targets must be on the same host and owned by the same user. if `jsatck` connects to a JVM of a different Java version, the behaviour is undefined: if `jstack`cannot print well-formated stack traces due to VM incompatibilities, it will print the raw data in human-readable form.
This differs from the HotSpot version of `jstack`, which allows access to remote hosts and will display data from core dumps. OpenJ9's `jstack` displays information about only local processes owned by the current user, due to security considerations. A user may display remote processes using `ssh jstack ...`. To view information from a core dump, `jdmpview` is preferred. Other options , such as `-F` (force a dump of an unresponsive) may be accomplished using `kill -QUIT <pid>`. Printing of native stack frames is not supported due to limitations of the VM.

issue_title: Allow non-vTable methods to be added/removed during class replacement
description:
The addition or removal of methods which do not affect the shape of the vTable should be allowed in fast HCR.
Methods which never appear in the vTable are:
- private instance methods
- static methods
Methods which do not need to appear in the vTable but currently do:
- final instance methods which do not override
New final methods should follow the invokeprivate path. This is likely a matter of removing their vTable modifier and modifying the restrictions on which methods can use invokeprivate during resolution.

issue_title: Eclipse IDE crashes with -Xverify:none
description:
I recently learned about OpenJ9 and I wanted to start using it. However I experienced systematic crashes when doing a full clean/build of my projects in eclipse.
I eventually narrowed it down to the `-Xverify:none` switch, which I can see is not supported by OpenJ9: Should OpenJ9 ignore it if this is harmful?
I'm sure a lot of people running eclipse with hotspot have that switch on, it's been documented for years as an option to set to speed up eclipse.
As a reference, this is my custom eclipse switches that I had with hotspot:
-Xmn512m
-Xss2m
-Xverify:none
-Xms1024m
-Xmx3072m
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:+UseStringDeduplication
This is what I now use with OpenJ9 and seems to be stable:
-Xss2m
-Xms1024m
-Xmx3072m
-Xtune:virtualized
-Xshareclasses:cacheDir=C:\dev\eclipses\shared-classes

issue_title: GPF in j9vm29.dll with openj9-0.12.0 on Windows Server 2016
description:
Hello,
We have a GPF (Global Protection Fault) crash of one of our Java utility running with AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.2 with OpenJ9 on Windows Server 2016, with a java dump showing that it occurred in j9vm29.dll.
I found the following page from an IBM site giving some hints about how to analyze the related Java dump:
Based on this page, my understanding is that the crash took place in j9vm29.dll library which is part of the OpenJ9 JVM, and we have no JNI in our Java application.
This issue is not systematic, and when it occurred, the machine's memory usage wasn't heavy, and we found no interesting events in Windows events logs.
Here's the java full file:
[javacore.20190227.222307.7284.0002.txt](
if this crash report isn't sufficient for OpenJ9 developers to spot where the issue is, then would you please let me know what kind options I could add to 'java' command to get more traces in case this crash takes place again?
Kind regards,
Alexandre Vermeerbergen

This needs to be fixed such that cudaInfo is only freed after it is not needed anymore.

issue_title: AArch64: Fails to build when OpenSSL is enabled
description:
Build of AArch64 runtime fails if you specify `--with-openssl=fetched` in running `configure`.

issue_title: Format z/OS errno2 values for OOME at j.l.Thread.start()
description:
The exception detail message for OutOfMemoryError at `java.lang.Thread.start()` on z/OS reports the errno2 value as a 64-bit hex value. For example:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to create a thread: retVal -1073741830, errno 132 (<hex>), errno2 -1055784930 (<hex>) at java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:982) at HelloWorld3.main(HelloWorld3.java:51)
It would be more user-friendly to report the errno2 as the lower 8 hex digits only, <hex> in the example above. The decimal value is not used on z/OS for any of the errno2 documentation nor for the error code diagnostic tools such as `edcmtext` or `bpxmtext`. The high 8 hex digits are not used and because the are all <hex> they make the errno2 value look like a negative number, which is confusing.
The z/OS documentation confirms that only the lower 8 hex digits are signficant for errno2 values. For example:
> The range of values for the XL C/C++ runtime library is 0X'C0000000' through 0X'CFFFFFFF'.

issue_title: Porting OpenJ9 to RISC-V
description:
We determined to port a complete runtime environment including OpenJDK11 + OpenJ9 + OMR (without JIT) to the RISC-V development board (e.g. HiFive Unleashed with Linux support / please refer to for details) to get it work on the board.
According to the explanation of RISC-V cross-compilers at the JDK /JRE is supposed to be executed with Linux support in the user mode as the JVM /application is multiple-threaded.
Overall, there are a bunch of prerequisites before compiling OpenJ9:
- the Freedom E SDK ( + openOCD ready for use (already offered on the website at - compile a cross compiler with glibc support: e.g. riscv-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc based on the instructions at if OK, check whether it works good with simple test.
- probably need the Yocto build system ( or to build everything including a Linux/RISC-V kernel ( a root file system image, a bootloader, a toolchain, QEMU, etc.
- (to be added if anything else)
Considering the complexity & unexpected challenges during the porting, the project will be split into at least 4 sub-tasks as follows to be accomplished to achieve our goal:
- compile a build without JIT on Linux (changed all request config/setting to get it work) to ensure it works good as expected; if everything goes well, all changes will be added to the compilation with riscv-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc.
- import the FFI code (libffi) for RISC-V support to OpenJ9 ( / need to open an Eclipse CQ for that)
- figure out whether we need to modify the related config/setting in the Freedom E SDK and how to integrate them into the config/setting in OpenJDK11 + OpenJ9 + OMR to ensure the build is compiled with riscv-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc.
- might need to run via an Emulator (e.g. QEMU) on the host to ensure it works before uploading.
- figure out how to flash/upload the compiled build & the Linux port to the development board to get it executed/tested.
- (to be added if anything else)
The issue at #11136 was created separately to track the progress of OpenJ9 JIT on RISC-V.
Another issue at for the CI pipline environment setup.
FYI: @DanHeidinga , @pshipton, @tajila

issue_title: OpenJ9 / OMR fails to build on AIX when using latest XLC v16.1
description:
In OpenJDK jdk branch (jdk13) and hence the jdk13 extensions repository there have been changes to use xlclang/xlclang++ if available on AIX systems.
If XLC 16.1 is installed then xlclang/xlclang++ is provided and used when building OpenJ9/OMR.
When using xlclang/xlclang++ there are quite a lot of compiler/linker options that are not supported anymore and cause the build to fail. This website shows all the options that are unsupported: The makefiles for OpenJ9 and OMR need to be modified to not use these unsupported options.

issue_title: Having a NFS home directory gives confusing shared cache error message
description:
If the user's home directory is set to a network (NFS) location, trying to use/create a shared cache results in the following error, which is cryptic. Better to have an error which is understandable, without having to look any further.
`JVMSHRC404E Failed to get a directory for the cache`
Further, this message code has the following explanation, which isn't appropriate for all the failure cases.
`J9NLS_SHRC_OSCACHE_GETCACHEDIR_FAILED.explanation=The directory path requested is bigger than the internal buffer space`

issue_title: Use 1MB as native thread stack size minimum on 64-bit z/OS
description:
As the smallest possible native stack size on 64-bit z/OS is 1MB, could the handling of -Xmso and the default native stack size change to use 1MB as the minimum native stack size?
At the time of writing, the default native stack size value used is 256KB for non-compressed references JVM and 384KB for compressed refs. This leads to artificial native OOME's when the JVM predicts that the native stack is about to grow above these values. In truth, there is no OOM condition until the native stack grows to 1MB, because that is the smallest native thread stack possible on z/OS 64-bit.

issue_title: Include J9VMThread in `!info thread` output in jdmpview
description:
The `!stackslots` output is usually the most important output to begin investigating a dump on exception. It requires the `J9VMThread` of the thread throwing the exception.
The only way I know how to get this is to first do `!info thread` to get the thread that's executing, but this does not have the `J9VMThread`, instead it has the Thread object and posix thread id.
To get the `J9VMThread` we need to run `!threads` and then correlate the posix thread id with the appropriate thread to get the `J9VMThread`.
It would be more efficient to simply include the `J9VMThread` in the `info thread` output.

Calls to ManagementFactory.getXXXMXBean are significantly more expensive on Java 11 & 12 than Java 8. Here are some example outputs (each item is `time java Ut`):

Java 12

getMbean: 214
getName: 0
getUptime: 0

user 0m0.512s

Java 12
26538@alasdaismbp3089.war.can.ibm.com uptime: 231
getMbean: 63
getName: 46
getUptime: 1

It is possible that on hotspot the classes are being initialized sooner, but uptime (returned from the RuntimeMXBean.getUptime is higher in the OpenJ9 case and while that could be due to implementation details the time output from the shell suggests that OpenJ9 is taking much longer.
Diagnostic files
The test code

public class Ut {

 System.out.println("getMbean: " + (st2 - st));
 System.out.println("getName: " + (st3 - st2));
 System.out.println("getUptime: " + (st4 - st3));
 }
}

issue_title: Different result presented in os.arch between openjdk and openj9 on Mac
description:
I realized that `os.arch` is different between openjdk and openj9 on Mac. On Linux, they return the same `os.arch`.
$ /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/jdk1.8.0_181.jdk/Contents/Home/bin/java -XshowSettings:all
...
 os.arch = x86_64
...
$ /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/adoptopenjdk-8-openj9.jdk/Contents/Home/bin/java -XshowSettings:all
...
 os.arch = amd64
...
This difference causes [an JNI link error]( in Spark. This is because `zstd-jni` determines [dll path]( by using `os.arch` as a part of the path name.

Summary of problem
There is a native crash occurring in the JVM when attempting to read an image. I can reproduce the issue with a fairly simple Java app, though it does require me to load some native libraries. I am still working to identify it there is a specific native library that reveals this issue. The conditions seem to be the following -
1. The Java class loads some native libraries via `System.loadLibrary()`. Without this, step 2 works without issues.
2. The Java class calls `javax.imageio.ImageIO#read(java.io.File)`. This Java method internally loads some native libraries in the JVM (due to static initializer in java.awt.Toolkit class). This line causes the JVM to crash.

issue_title: JVMTI agent is unable to get Java version in native code on OpenJ9 JDK 12
description:
We use JVMTI's GetSystemProperty function to get Java version as a number like 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 etc. in native code, in an early phase when no Java code has loaded yet. Since OpenJ9 Java 12 this approach no longer works.
Property "java.vm.version" on HotSpot returns something like "12.0.1+12" which we can parse to get the version. OpenJ9 returns "openj9-0.14.0" which is useless for our purpose because it indicates the entire release with different Java versions like Java 11, Java 12 etc.
Property "java.vm.specification.version" returns "11" on OpenJ9 Java 11, and we can parse it. Unfortunately, OpenJ9 Java 12 returns an empty string.
Neither can we use JVMTI's GetVersionNumber function because for Java 11 and Java 12 it returns the same value JVMTI_VERSION_11 = 300B0000.
Could you please make "java.vm.specification.version" return a meaningful value ("12"), or suggest a workaround.

issue_title: OpenJ9 Locking Revamp: A Scalable Design
description:
Below, I have listed the five different approaches/solutions, which will improve OpenJ9's locking performance. Each approach listed below will incrementally improve OpenJ9's locking performance. ## Transition to a Scalable Lock
**Unfavorable environment**: OpenJ9 performance regressions are seen on large machines (24+ CPUs) with high lock contention where many threads attempt to acquire a lock simultaneouly.
In the [OpenJ9 three-tier spin loops]( we use TATAS locks; CAS operation is performed only when the lock is not held.
TATAS locks collapse in the above described environment (refer to **Figure 3** in [MCS Lock Now Welcomes Guests](
For [Scalable Syncronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors]( we need to move away from TATAS locks since they are dangerous and can cause system performance to suddenly collapse in real workloads.
I am proposing a move to queue based locks. The Linux kernel has replaced non-scalable locks with MCS locks. There are different variants of the MCS locks:
1. **MCS lock:** refer to section 2.4 in [Scalable Syncronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors](
2. **K42 lock:** variant of the MCS locks that requires fewer API changes, [patented by IBM]( 3. **CLH lock:** variant of the MCS lock where the waiter spins on its predecessor.
4. **HCLH lock:** hierarchical variant of the CLH lock inttended for NUMA machines.
5. **[qspinlock]( MCS with 32-bit lock-words (designed for kernels), requires kernel-space ability to disable preemption.
6. **MCSg**: MCS for regular users and TATAS for guest (infrequent) users who don't need the lock context; refer to section 2 in [MCS Lock Now Welcomes Guests](
7. **MCSg: more fair version of MCSg.
**Lock comparison studies:**
1. [MCS Lock Now Welcomes Guests, 2016](
 - Compares TATAS, K42, K42-TLS, CLH, CLH-TLS, MCS, MCSg, MCSg++, MCSg+.
2. [Non-scalable locks are dangerous, 2012](
 - Compares ticket lock, MCS lock, CLH lock, proportional lock, K42 lock.
**When moving to queue based locks, we need to**
- Replace the [three-tier TATAS spinloops]( with the queue based lock algorithms.
- Check compatibility with the [lock nursery]( (32-bit lock words) and [lock reservation]( features in OpenJ9.
- Amend OpenJ9's [adaptive spinning feature]( to support MCS or disable it.
- Re-purpose spin parameters to support MCS locks because they utilize spinning as well.
The [code/implementation]( for the various lock algorithms (TATAS, MCS, K42, bitlist-lock, stack-lock, ticket-lock, etc.).
**Which queue based locking algorithm to use?** Criteria - ease of acceptance and performance benefits. Choice: TBD.
## Lock Cohorting
[Lock Cohorting: A General Technique for Designing NUMA Locks](
The above research paper discusses about "scalable NUMA aware locking algorithms. Lock cohorting allows one to transform any spin-lock algorithm, with minimal nonintrusive changes, into a scalable NUMA-aware spin-lock. Cohort detection property: a thread releasing the lock can detect if it has a nonempty cohort of threads concurrently attempting to acquire the lock. A NUMA-aware cohort lock consists of a single thread-oblivious global lock and a set of local locks, one for each NUMA node. The local locks must provide the cohort detect property. Results demonstrate that cohort locks perform as well or better than known locks when the load is low and significantly out-perform them as the load increases."
**Comparison of various locking algorithms:** refer to **Figures 7, 8 and 9** in the above research paper.
Lock cohorting yields better results than just using queue based locks.
## Concurrency Restriction
[Malthusian Locks](
**Summary of the above research paper:**
**ACS** - Active Circulating Thread Set
**LWS** - Lock Working Set
**LWSS** - Lock Working Set Size
Applications running in modern multi-threaded environments are sometimes over-threaded. The excess threads do not improve performance, and in fact may act to degrade performance via scalability collapse. We leverage the existence of such locks by modifying the lock admission policy so as to intentionally limit (a.k.a concurrency restriction) the number of distinct threads circulating over the lock in a given period. **Objective function:** minimize the size of the ACS (and thus the LWSS) while still remaining work conserving, ensuring there are sufficient threads in the ACS to saturate the lock – and that the critical section enjoys maximum occupancy. Two metrics for short-term fairness, which help gauge the trade-off between the throughput and fairness, are used:
- Average LWSS over the measurement interval
- Median time to reacquire (MTTR), computed over the entire acquisition history
## Transactional Lock Elision (TLE)
[Refined Transactional Lock Elision](
TLE uses hardware transcational memory (HTM) to introduce concurrency in existing locking algorithms. In the above research paper, **Figure 1** highlights the base design for TLE and refined TLE. Section 2 lists the TLE related works. Section 3 (RW-TLE) and Section 4 (FG-TLE) contain two different TLE algorithms. 2x to 4x speedup is seen with the proposed TLE approaches.
## Scalable Statistics Counters
[Scalable Statistics Counters](
In high contention scenarios, I have seen the Java Lock Monitor (JLM) counters overflow. Also, we update the JLM counters every-time while exiting a three-tier spinloop. The inefficiency (poor performance) in updating the JLM counters increase the time spent in monitor_enter and monitor_exit functions, especially in high contention cases.
The above paper proposes scalable statistics counters. These perform well in NUMA environments, have minimal space overhead and don't need to be updated every time (i.e. less CAS operations). Such counters rely on probability models, they are near-accurate and yield 100x+ throughput in comparison to naive/traditional counters. They use the principles of [Morris's Counting Algorithm]( 255 is the largest numerical value, which can be stored in a 8-bit counter; using Morris's algorithm, the largest value represented by a 8-bit counter can be 130,000. There is trade-off between accuracy and performance.

issue_title: OpenJ9 cannot load/find/link .jnilib files on macOS; when renamed to .dylib, it works
description:
When running some applications with OpenJ9 that depend on some Java Native Interface stuff on macOS, OpenJ9 seems to not be able to load those dependencies when they're called `<something>.jnilib`. It will load them when one renames or links to the files with a `<something>.dylib` name.
Here's some error output from Tanuki wrapper as used within Anypoint Studio (an Eclipse based IDE):

Starting the Mule Container...

WrapperManager: following files:
WrapperManager: libwrapper-macosx-universal-64.dylib
WrapperManager: libwrapper.dylib
WrapperManager: could be located on the following java.library.path:
WrapperManager: /Applications/Anypoint Studio 7.app/Contents/Eclipse/configuration/org.eclipse.osgi/506/data/.runtimes/tooling-em0uavkj/lib/boot
WrapperManager: Please see the documentation for the wrapper.java.library.path
WrapperManager: configuration property.
WrapperManager: Writing to the backend pipe failed (35): Resource temporarily unavailable
Pipe send failed. Incomplete. Sent 8051 of 15226 bytes.

Note the extension. Renaming or linking to the file makes the wrapper work. This problem does not occur on Hotspot.

issue_title: Java 13, deprecate -Xverify:none and -noverify
description:
The following OpenJDK Java 13 change in the release notes Deprecated Java Options -Xverify:none and -noverify (JDK-8214719)
hotspot/runtime
The Java options -Xverify:none and -noverify have been deprecated in this release. The options will continue to work as intended in this release but will generate the following warning when used:
`warning: Options -Xverify:none and -noverify were deprecated in version 13.0 and will likely be removed in a future release.`
Deprecating these options helps prevent users from running code that violates the JVM Specification, which can leave their applications open to malicious code.
Users who need to run without startup verification can use AppCDS to archive their classes. The classes will get verified during archiving and so avoid verification at runtime.
Note that if you encounter issues while using either of these options, it is very likely that you will be required to reproduce the problem without using these options before Oracle Support can assist with an investigation.

issue_title: DDR JIT stack walker takes insufficient parameters
description:
The `!jitstack` and `!jitstackslots` command in DDR are used to start the stack walk at a JIT frame by providing sufficient root values to walk the stack.
Currently, the root values are `vmThread`, `SP`, `PC` and (optionally) `ELS`. For a complete walk, values for `j2iFrame` and `i2jState` must also be provided (like `ELS`, they are currently inferred from the vmThread). The two new args should be added as optional.
`j2iFrame` is either `NULL` (if no jit->interp transition has ever taken place) or the `BP` value of the `j2i` frame.
`i2jState` starts off pointing to the `ELS i2jState`, but is updated to point into the `j2i` frame each time one is seen.
Almost all real-world uses of these extensions target a JIT frame very near the top of the stack, so this has not been an issue.
creator: gacholio

issue_title: SharedClasses: Improve timestamping story - no assumption that Jar files are kept open
description:
Making available here the IBM design that resulted in the JVM_ZipHook implementation ( Introduction One of the main features of the Shared Classes component is its "dynamic update" capability. If a class changes on the filesystem, we detect this and ensure that the correct class is always returned from the cache or loaded from disc. This is an absolutely essential feature as it guarantees transparency when running with shared classes. The main problem with keeping track of class and jar file version is the performance impact of having to check every element on the classpath before a class is loaded. We optimize this as much as possible by stating the assumption (in the Helper API documentation) that once a Jar file has been opened for reading by a ClassLoader, it should be kept open for the life of the ClassLoader. By forcing the first class-load from each jar to come from disk, regardless of whether it is in the cache or not, we get the classloader to lock jar files for us. We keep track of which jars on a given classpath are locked and once they are locked, we assume that they cannot change and stop checking them. Without this optimization, stat'ing each entry on the classpath when we load every class is prohibitively expensive. It's actually more complicated than this, because for directory entries on a classpath, there is nothing to lock. We have to mock up expected sub-directories and class name for a class file to see if one has "appeared". This too is expensive and having many directories on a classpath has an inevitable impact on performance. There is also a second problem. Bug Title: Missing Java 2 security permissions when using the Attach API
Bug Description: Java -version output
I don't have `java -version` output, but this is the java version info from the Liberty log header:
java.home = /home/jazz_build/_DAkcIIgiEem3a_lXnKb_ZA-EBC.PROD.WASRTC-40H-000-00-00/jbe/jvms/OpenJDK11U-jdk_x64_linux_openj9_11.0.2_9_openj9-0.12.1
java.version = 11.0.2
java.runtime = OpenJDK Runtime Environment (11.0.2+9)
os = Linux (4.4.0-131-generic; amd64) (en_US)
As the java.home path implies, this uses JDK 11.0.2+9 using OpenJ9-0.12.1. This is using a released version (not some internal/nightly build).
Summary of problem
We are using the standard JDK attach API to self-attach to a running VM, but when Java 2 security is enabled, we get a permission error for something that the JDK should be giving itself permission to do (possibly via `$JAVA_HOME/conf/security/java.policy`).

issue_title: 64-bit z/OS Java SDK allows Xmso values less than the smallest possible native stack of 1M
description:
As the smallest possible native stack size on 64-bit z/OS is 1MB, the default Xmso value was increased from 256/384K to 1M in issue [5156](
However, applications that have historically set Xmso values <1M are still exposed to future failures as the JRE validates native stack frames used using whatever the Xmso value is set to.
As an example if Xmso128K is set, then the JVM will fail if too many stack frames are used such as if starting a debug session, when in-fact on the 64bit z/OS JVM the LE stack is a min of 1M in size and allocated in a min of 1M segments, so plenty of native storage is actually available See [LE Programming Ref](
creator: PhilWakelin

issue_title: Footprint regressions when using -XX:+TransparentHugePage
description: Transparent huge page support was added to OMR via Subsequent performance testing indicates that using this support (which may be enabled by default on Linux until the introduction of #6013) can negatively impact footprint measurements. In particular, a footprint regression of 8% was found on pLinux with the OS setting of /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage set to madvise, compared to a build without madvise(..., MADV_HUGEPAGE) support.
creator: pshipton

issue_title: OpenJ9 super-slow with libasan (address santizer) versus HotSpot
description:
Hello,
We tried to move our C++ test tools based on ASAN (see for background on this tools) to detect memory leaks/freed memory pointers/etc from Hotspot Java to OpenJ9 Java.
We have JNI code, therefore we need to provide a Java Runtime to our test factory.
When we switched this Java Runtime dependency from AdoptOpenJDK 11 based on HotSpot to AdoptOpenJDK 11 based on OpenJ9, it became so slow that we had to rollback.
We have isolated a trivial test case to reproduce this issue, showing that with HotSpot it takes less than 1 second to run 'java -version' with LIBASAN, while it takes more than 4 minutes to run the same test with OpenJ9.
Prerequisites:
- Operating system: CentOS 7.5
- We install AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.1 with HotSpot in ./hotspot/jdk-11.0.3+7
- We install AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.1 with OpenJ9 in ./openj9/jdk-11.0.3+7
- We use package libasan5-8.2.1-3.el7.x86_64
We run the following test:
export LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib64/libasan.so.5
time ./hotspot/jdk-11.0.3+7/bin/java -version
time ./openj9/jdk-11.0.3+7/bin/java -version
Hotspot result:
...
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 23284 byte(s) leaked in 158 allocation(s).
real 0m0.50s
user 0m0.17s
sys 0m0.34s
OpenJ9 result:
...
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 947030 byte(s) leaked in 337 allocation(s).
real 4m2.17s
user 0m20.25s
sys 3m41.96s
This huge execution time difference clearly excludes the use of OpenJ9 to check the memory errors of our C++ code depending on Java through JNI, which is too bad.
Is there a way to get this execution time difference fixed? any JVM option which I could use to make this usage of OpenJ9-based JavaRuntime actually usable?
Kind regards,
Alexandre Vermeerbergen

description:

issue_title: PR Groovy pipeline scripts are slow
description:
I've been noticing a slowdown in the amount of time it takes to launch PR builds since the switch to pipeline generated jobs. For example a build triggered via `Jenkins test extended all jdk8,jdk11` produces the build seen in [1]. Inside each "Processing DSL script buildenv/jenkins/jobs/pipelines/Pipeline_Template.groovy" step seems to take roughly 2:30 min. for each job that is being generated.
For this particular case there are many jobs, so we end up waiting roughly one hour between requesting the tests via a PR comment and any build jobs being launched. Was wondering if something can be done to improve the performance of these pipelines so that we reach the build step faster.

issue_title: Class Unloading in Scavenger possibility
description:
In Gencon GC policy Class Unloading is not available in Local GC (Scavenger) currently. The Class Unloading is one of the most common reasons to percolate to Global GC, particularly for applications using "reflect" heavily. An unloading of classes in Scavenger might reduce number of Global GCs dramatically in some cases. An unloading for classes is done on classloader level - so if non of classloader classes instances are alive the classloader can be unloaded. (There is an exception for Anonymous classes treated specially).
There is obvious that Scavenger can make decision about classloader unloading if all instances of all it's classes are located in Nursery only (has no information about liveness objects in the Tenure). This can be controlled by adding special flag to classloader "has_Instances_In_Tenure". Set this flag to "off" at classloader creation time initially. In Gencon there are only two ways to get object in Tenure: direct allocation in Tenure (out-of-line path) and tenuring of object in Scavenger. In both cases "has_Instances_In_Tenure" flag should be set to object->class->classloader. So the only classloaders with "has_Instances_In_Tenure" flag is not set might be subject for class unloading in Scavenger.
Classloader can be unloaded if non of its class instances are alive. This can be controlled by using classloader object location. It should be allocated in Nursery initially and be attempted to be copied every time we scan copied instance of any of its classes. (Class object can be copied at the same time as well or its copy operation can be postponed to Clearable phase).
Class unloading in Scavenger Clearable phase would look like: if classloader flag "has_Instances_In_Tenure" is not set (instances in Nursery only) and its classloader object located in Survivor part of the Nursery (non of its instances have been copied so non of them are alive) this classloader can be unloaded.
Note: classloader object can be tenured because of its age naturally - in this case class unloading would be possible in Global GC only. There are two possibilities here - either it is almost irrelevant because we can try to address unloading for short living classloaders/classes created by "reflect" or we can artificially prolong life for classloader objects in the Nursery.
Also classloader object can be tenured if any of class instances are tenured. However "has_Instances_In_Tenure" still be necessary in this case because it does not cover object allocation path.
Setting flag "has_Instances_In_Tenure" (if it has not been set yet) for each tenured object might be a possible performance concern (but should not be too bad IMO)

issue_title: Support the `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` option
description:
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError on Hotspot just terminates without creating any diagnostic files. If you add options to create diagnostic files like -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError the files are created before terminating.
The implementation would be to exit on any java.lang.OutOfMemoryError whether thrown by the VM or by user code.
The "exit check" would have to be after the hook that generates the diagnostic files as the OpenJ9 equivalent of `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError ` is the default
creator: DanHeidinga
text:

Bug Description: -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError on Hotspot just terminates without creating any diagnostic files. If you add options to create diagnostic files like -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError the files are created before terminating.
The implementation would be to exit on any java.lang.OutOfMemoryError whether thrown by the VM or by user code.
The "exit check" would have to be after the hook that generates the diagnostic files as the OpenJ9 equivalent of `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError ` is the default

issue_title: Add missing jcmd options
description:
Add:
- `-f`: read commands from a file
- select VMs by main class instead of VMID
- select all VMs if VMID==0
Update help text accordingly:
jcmd <vmid | class> <arguments>
...
 <main class>: string used to select processes from the full list; may be a substring of a fully qualified class name
...
 -f <command file>: read command from a file, one command per line
...
 A <vmid> of 0 indicates that the command should be applied to all Java processes. This is part of Doc issue eclipse/openj9-docs#343

issue_title: finalFieldSetAllowed doing validation on class file with version less than 53
description:
In `resolvesupport.cpp` the brief for the `finalFieldSetAllowed` states:
In class files with version 53 or later, setting of final fields is only allowed from initializer methods.
 which implies that the check should not happen in class files with version 52 or less.
In the check to do the validation is changed:
The old condition calls the function `ramClassChecksFinalStores` which includes a check for class file version >= 53, while the new condition does not do this check and runs the validation on all class file versions.
Ran into this when investigating

issue_title: jcmd help output is not sufficient
description:
Format:
 jcmd <vmid> <arguments>
 Arguments:
 <vmid>: Attach API VM ID as shown in jps or other Attach API-based tools.
 command[command arguments]: command from the list returned by "-help"
 -help: print the list of diagnostic commands
- It's not obvious that `jcmd <vmid> help` prints the available commands. - How do you get help on the individual commands? i.e. `help Dump.heap` works
- When you run `jcmd <vmid>` without any command it results in an error. It may be useful to have this print the available commands.
creator: pshipton

issue_title: Add DDR memory remap facility
description:
For certain debugging situations, structures may be copied into malloc'ed memory. It would be nice to be able to use DDR generically in these cases by allowing the user to remap blocks of memory. Something like:
> remap address,size,newAddress
Any bytes read from memory between address and address+size-1 should be read from a base of newAddress instead.
Ideally, we should allow an arbitrary number of remaps, and there should be commands to list and remove them (listmaps, unmap perhaps).

issue_title: Dockerfile for buildenv jdk11 x86_64 image uses jdk10
description:
[Dockerfile for **jdk11** x86_64]( installs **jdk 10** to this folder: **/root/bootjdk10**
The relevant section of the dockerfile:
# Download and install boot JDK from AdoptOpenJDK
RUN cd /root \
 && wget -O bootjdk10.tar.gz " \
 && tar -xzf bootjdk10.tar.gz \
 && rm -f bootjdk10.tar.gz \
 && mv $(ls | grep -i jdk) bootjdk10
# Set environment variable JAVA_HOME, and prepend ${JAVA_HOME}/bin to PATH
ENV JAVA_HOME="/root/bootjdk10"

issue_title: PR builds are inconsistent
description:
Both the build and test jobs in a PR test pipeline use the `pull/nnn/merge` reference: the problem is the meaning of that reference can change between when the build is launched and when the test portion begins. See where the build was based on `98a888ab596c4cec379318bd9ae192ae633f3a9b`, but the test was based on `15afcbb98d2f683190b07ca803e189749b6c64c5` because in the interim, #6938 was merged which changed the meaning of `pull/6822/merge`. The result in [1] is errors that refer to lines that don't exist in the commit used to build.
[1]

issue_title: Rename libjvm.so in compressedrefs and default directories
description:
Apparently, cmake does not distinguish between the shared libraries (all called 'libjvm.so') in the compressedrefs, j9vm and server directories. If it fixes on the one in the compressedrefs (or, presumably, the default) directory, link errors ensue because that version does not have a reference to libdl.so. See for more detail.
The shared library in the compressedrefs directory doesn't have the same behavior as the other shared libraries of the same name: I propose we change the name of the library that appears in the compressedrefs (or default) directory to avoid this confusion.

issue_title: Remove dummy leaf pointer in Arraylet
description:
Currently GC allocates extra leaf pointer in Arraylet spine in case if size of Array is times of Arraylet leaf size. GC initializes this pointer to NULL. This hack was necessary because Builder helper caches next leaf pointer if reading of current leaf is complete. In the case if Arraylet spine is a last object in the heap "next" address might be not in committed memory. We are not using Builder for many years and seems nothing in GC or VM requires this hack any more. I would like to delete this code if possible.
May I ask JIT Team double check is any code rely on this "dummy for read" pointer?
Removing this hack is a part of cleaning Arraylet logic required for Arraylet Double Mapping optimization. @DanHeidinga @pshipton @andrewcraik FYI

issue_title: Apache Flink fails to start with OpenJ9 versions of AdoptOpenJDK because 'T' unit is not supported by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize
description:
Hello,
While trying to run Apache Flink with AdoptOpenJDK with OpenJ9 instead of AdopOpenJDK with HotSpot, the JVM failed to start with the following error:
[root@ip-10-8-29-86 flink]# cat flink-flink-taskexecutor-0-ip-10-8-29-86.eu-west-2.compute.internal.out
JVMJ9VM013W Initialization error in function VMInitStages(0): Parse error for -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize= - option malformed.
Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.
Error: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.
We found that this error occurs because Apache Flink starts the JVM with the following option: XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=8388607T**, and this is hard-coded, as one can see at line 65 of And the root cause seems to be that OpenJ9 does not supports '**T**' (Terabytes) unit, see for example with a recent nightly build of AdoptOpenJDK 11 on Linux:
$ ./java -version
openjdk version "11.0.5" 2019-10-15
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.5+9-201910091831)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build master-531d15d38, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20191009_352 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 531d15d38
OMR - 606cb8e9
JCL - 642d34017c based on jdk-11.0.5+9)
$ ./java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1T -version
JVMJ9VM013W Initialization error in function VMInitStages(0): Parse error for -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize= - option malformed.
Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.
Error: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.
whereas this variant works:
$ ./java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1024G -version
openjdk version "11.0.5" 2019-10-15
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.5+9-201910091831)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build master-531d15d38, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20191009_352 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 531d15d38
OMR - 606cb8e9
JCL - 642d34017c based on jdk-11.0.5+9)
and HotSpot has no issue with "T" unit:
$ ./java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=1T -version
openjdk version "11.0.5" 2019-10-15
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.5+9-201910091809)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.5+9-201910091809, mixed mode)
We can by-pass this OpenJ9 issue by patching our Apache Flink installation.
Anyway, would it be possible to fix OpenJ9 to make it support '**T**' unit, so as to avoid future adopters to fall into that trap and maybe discard OpenJ9 as a viable alternative to Hotpot? Kind regards,
Alexandre Vermeerbergen

issue_title: Support non-tenured objects in the constantpool
description:
JDK 11 introduced ConstantDynamic which allowed user allocated objects to be installed in classes ConstantPools (CP). This required changes to the GC so that the scavenges would scan the CP of classes with ConstantDynamics.
Our current JSR 292 implementation forces MethodType and MethodHandle objects that are stored into the CP to be tenured. Given we have the capability to scan CPs in scavenges, it would be good to remove the special case code to tenure MT & MH.
This also is an enabler for the investigation work in #7352 (Use OpenJDK LambdaForm MH implementation) as it makes it easier to consume the OpenJDK classes without patches.
Ideally, the existing store barriers would be sufficient to mark the classes as having CP entries that are in the young gen. The existing special handling for Condy can be seen in If we need to do special casing, then the following cases would need special handling:
* `J9CPTYPE_METHOD_TYPE`
* `J9CPTYPE_METHODHANDLE`
* `J9CPTYPE_CONSTANT_DYNAMIC`
Additionally, for classes loaded by Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass() and using constantpool patching, we would also need to scan `J9CPTYPE_STRING` as they can be used to "smuggle" other objects into the CP.

issue_title: Integer overflow when increasing the capacity of very large StringBuffers
description:
The OpenJ9 StringBuffer class behaves very differently to the OpenJDK StringBuffer class when appending small numbers of characters to very large StringBuffers (half of the maximum capacity of `Integer.MAX_VALUE`).
Consider this testcase, which appends characters to a StringBuffer one at a time, and prints out the capacity of the StringBuffer whenever it increases:
public class StringBufferTest {
 public static void main(String[] args) {
 StringBuffer b = new StringBuffer();
 int cap = b.capacity();
 while(true) {
 b.append("a");
 if (b.capacity() > cap) {
 cap = b.capacity();

On the plus side, this means that more characters can be appended to the StringBuffer on OpenJ9 before it throws an OOM. However, we have recently seen a situation where this behaviour prolonged the suffering of an application which was malfunctioning and appending too many characters to a StringBuffer - the repeated copying of the backing array to a slightly larger backing array can be extremely expensive in a large multi-threaded application.
Regardless of the pros and cons, it looks like the OpenJ9 behaviour is not intentional. It happens when `newcapacity` overflows on line 762:
758 private void ensureCapacityImpl(int min) {

Which causes `newLength` to always be set to `min` on line 764. This means the backing array will grow only just enough to accommodate the character(s) being appended this time round, as seen in the testcase.
The OpenJDK code considers the potential overflow more carefully and prevents it, with the consequence that an OutOfMemoryError is thrown much earlier.
It may be that the OpenJ9 behaviour is preferable under some circumstances (maybe a command line flag is needed?). But in any case the behaviour should be intentional, not a consequence of a defect.

issue_title: Add static_assert support in the VM/GC makefiles
description:
As described in [1] we can have static_assert in the VM/GC by adding command line options to the compiler build process. These options are harmless and enable the use of valuable features such as `static_assert`. We need to find the right place where these options can be added in the VM/GC makefiles.
As part of this issue we should try and revert the x86-only portion of #7678 as a proof of concept that the change to enable `static_assert` is working.
[1]

issue_title: VM native lookupJava8Package() is redundant
description:
In `Java 9+ --illegal-access=permit` is turned on by default. This opens each package (that existed in `Java 8`) to ALL-UNNAMED unless `illegal-access=deny` is specified. This is for easy mitigation to modularity Java levels.
There is a `jdk8_packages.dat` [1] containing such `Java 8` packages to be exported to unnamed modules. `jdk.internal.module.ModuleBootstrap.addIllegalAccess()` [2] invokes `jdk.internal.module.IllegalAccessMaps.generate()` [3] which reads/parses/saves this dat file, and calls `jla.addOpensToAllUnnamed()` [4] for each package. This leads to which invokes for such packages.
Hence each `J9Package->exportToAllUnnamed` is set to true, and returns true for those `jdk8` packages at before hitting It appears there is no need to perform `lookupJava8Package()` within VM natives.

issue_title: Low-overhead Heap Profiling (JEP331) reports wrong allocation ratios
description:
Experimenting with the implementation of JEP331 that was introduced in the Java 12 variant of J9, we found the results are off by quite a lot. Since there seems to be a system to these values, a statistical anomaly can be ruled out. To reproduce I'm attaching a minimal JVMTI agent and a sample that shows the problem. We have also verified that the problem still persists in the most recent build. Sample:
The sample runs for a minute and alternately allocates two types, i.e., A and B. A contains one long (and is thus 16b - which also corresponds to jvmti getObjectSize) and B contains two longs, (24B). Since the object sampling interval is based on allocated memory (rather than objects) and due to the size ratio of B to A, we expect to get about 60% samples of Bs, and 40% samples of A, i.e., B objects are bigger, so it is more likely that B will be hit by random sample.
Agent:
The agent tags classes A and B on load, and maintains two static counters. It disregards all other objects that might get sampled. At the end, it prints the number of samples, and also the ratio between them. We expect to see something like 40% to 60% (within some margin of error), but we actually see consistently 50% to 50%.
Things we could already rule out:
*) Scalar replacement: We are adding all objects to an array list and clear it periodically to avoid scalar replacement. Also, on shutdown the agent forces a GC and makes a heap dump to show the actual distribution of objects, which shows more than 0 objects (meaning they are really being allocated) and a consistent distribution of 50% to 50%
*) Randomization: Since j9 doesnt randomize the sampling interval, the agent resets the interval with a random value at every sample. If it wouldn't, the samples would be off even more.
*) Interfering objects: Even when the agent samples other objects, the ratios of A to B should remain the same.
Things we already found out:
*) Collections matter: If the ratio is wrong and by how much it is wrong strongly depends on which collection we put the object into. Also the size of the collection matters, for example an array list with 1_000 capacity causes the correct ratios, with 1_000_000 elements the ratios are wrong. With a linked list, the ratios are completely off (0.5% As, 99.5% Bs). We understand that depending on the collection different JIT optimizations may be enabled, but even so, the heap dump we take shows the objects are indeed allocated in every case, meaning the ratios reported are wrong. Maybe there is a JIT optimization that doesn't properly respect heap sampling.
[Reproducer.zip](

issue_title: OpenJ9 JVM shouldn't unblock a signal by default
description:
Issue
Currently, all supported signals are unblocked during startup. A signal
is unblocked even when a signal handler is not installed for it. This
conflicts with an OpenJ9 consumer (e.g. a native app that embeds OpenJ9), which wants to block a set of signals. The OpenJ9 consumer blocks a
set of signals but the OMR signal library unblocks those signals at startup.
A signal should not be unblocked if it is not used i.e. a signal handler is not
registered for it.
 Recreating the failure
1) Download the micro-test: [micro_test.zip](
2) Run the micro-test:
cd micro_test
make run JVM_DIR=<PATH_TO_JAVA_HOME>
3) Raise `SIGUSR2`:
./stop <PID>
 Incorrect (bad) behavior
1. **make run JVM_DIR=<PATH_TO_JAVA_HOME>:**
[main] Starting JVM... OK.
[main] Java VM version: 1.8.0_232
[main] Waiting for signal...
[main] Now run ./stop 24072
2. **./stop 24072**
[stop] Sending SIGUSR2 to 24072
[stop] Termination signal set to 24072
 Expected (good) behavior
1. **make run JVM_DIR=<PATH_TO_JAVA_HOME>:**
[main] Starting JVM... OK.
[main] Java VM version: 1.8.0_232-internal
[main] Waiting for signal...
[main] Now run ./stop 24043
2. **./stop 24043**:
[stop] Sending SIGUSR2 to 24043
[stop] Termination signal set to 24043
[main] [signal_receiver] Signal 12 received.
[main] >>> Shutdown requested <<<
[main] Destroying JVM... OK.
[main] Shutdown successful!
 Good versus bad behavior
When `SIGUSR2` is raised via `./stop <PID>`, ...
... In the bad behavior, shutdown is not requested, and the JVM is not destroyed.
... In the good behavior, shutdown is requested, and the JVM is successfully destroyed.

issue_title: Sequential search of ROM class in Anonymous classes unloading
description: Anonymous classes unloading procedure uses sequential walk to find ROM class segment for each RAM class to be unloaded. It can be reason for performance degradation if number of Anonymous classes is large. Also with adding Anonymous classes support to SC searched ROM class can not be in the Anonymous classloader list at all, so it is worst case scenario

issue_title: Thread.suspend()/resume() deprecated for removal in Java 14
description:
Java 14 is deprecating Thread/ThreadGroup.suspend()/resume() for removal. OpenJ9 needs to add the deprecated flag to these methods for Java 14. In the future, tests which use these methods will need to be re-written or removed once the methods are removed.
 Thread.suspend()
 Thread.resume()
 ThreadGroup.suspend()
 ThreadGroup.resume()
 ThreadGroup.allowThreadSuspension(boolean)
These methods will be removed in a future release.

issue_title: Compilation errors with strncpy when compiling with GCC 9+
description:
The compilation warning `stringop-truncation` and `stringop-overflow ` were introduced since GCC 8.0. As a result, there are a bunch of code failures with these warnings (turned into error), mostly specific to `strncpy` on Open 9 & OMR when compiling with GCC > 8.0
e.g.
jvminitcommon.c: In function 'findDllLoadInfo':
jvminitcommon.c:38:2: error: 'strncpy' specified bound 64 equals destination size [-Werror=stringop-truncation]
 strncpy(key, dllName, SMALL_STRING_BUF_SIZE);
riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-g++ -DOPENJ9_BUILD -O3 -fno-strict-aliasing ...
 -DUT_DIRECT_TRACE_REGISTRATION -DTR_HOST_RISCV -c OSCache.cpp
OSCache.cpp: In static member function 'static IDATA SH_OSCache::removeCacheVersionAndGen(char*, UDATA, UDATA, const char*)':
OSCache.cpp:167:9: error: 'char* strncpy(char*, const char*, size_t)' specified bound depends on the length of the source argument [-Werror=stringop-overflow=]
 strncpy(buffer, nameStart, lengthMinusGen);
 ~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
To avoid these warnings, we need to figure out how to minimize the code change as it will impact all platforms regardless of GCC.
FYI: @keithc-ca, @DanHeidinga, @pshipton.
creator: ChengJin01

issue_title: Setup automatic trigger for Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-11
description:
Due to I've temporarily split OMR acceptance into 2 jobs, Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-8 (the original) and Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-11 (a new job). It seems this reduction in jobs starting at the same time is enough to allow git checkout on master to succeed. It worked well enough to get OMR promoted (manually) over the weekend.
Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-11 will start a bit later, but it needs to kick off automatically like Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-8 already does when there are new commits merged. To create Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-11 I copied Pipeline-OMR-Acceptance-8, but the automatic kick off isn't working, I assume it's configured in some other place.

issue_title: New Lock Reservation Option on Power
description:
Lock Reservation is currently only enabled to work with two classes: `StringBuffer` and `Random`. This experimental feature is an attempt to bring the optimization to a larger range classes through new heuristics to avoid expensive lock reservation cancellations.
The new lock reservation scheme will be largely behind the -XX:+GlobalLockReservation command line option. Without the option, the lock reservation system used will be very similar (but not identical due to unavoidable changes) to the original system.
The new lock reservation scheme adds a new Learning phase before a lock is reserved. During the Learning phase a lock reservation cancellation is not required if a second thread wishes to lock an object. If the Learning phase is successful, the object can be reserved.
If two threads attempt to lock the same object, then it can never be reserved again. Under the old system, lock reservation could be attempted again on the same object even after a reservation on the object was cancelled.
A system to bypass the new Learning state is added via new initial lockwords. Data is collected on a per class basis to try and predict if locked objects of that class will eventually go to Flat or Reserved. Based on that data, objects might go straight to Flat or Reserved when they are locked for the first time.
An improvement of 4% was seen on internal benchmarks from activating this feature.
The initial implementation of this feature will only work on Power. Future work will expand the feature to other platforms.

issue_title: LogManager initialization: Difference in behaviour between openj9 and hotspot
description:
We observed a difference in behaviour between openj9 and hotspot when it comes to initializing logging. Related: This difference was observed when we tried to run Quarkus tests against both implementations. Quarkus tests depend on a JBoss implementation of LogManager, some core tests check for it, assertThat(logManager).isInstanceOf(org.jboss.logmanager.LogManager.class). Because of the way that the Quarkus testing is setup, where the preferred LogManager (a jboss implementation) is not set up initially, but in a later pom file, we were seeing that by that time, openj9 had already loaded the default java.util.logging.LogManager, while hotspot seems to lazily initialize the jboss LogManager. As a current workaround to this, we set that system property at JVM startup.
Raising this as a potential issue of interest for the openj9 project, as it may be that other applications make assumptions about LogManager initialization behaviour, and it may be beneficial to lazily initialize also.
Note: this is not something that is flagged as an issue during conformance testing.
Note: Think we have also seen in the past (though the tests have been subsequently updated) that some openjdk (jtreg) tests assume that logging is lazily initialized, which was causing openj9 to fail those tests. We will have to dig to find these examples again.

issue_title: JEP-370 Foreign-Memory Access API
description:
JEP-370 Foreign-Memory Access API (Incubator)
> The foreign-memory access API will initially be provided as an incubating module, named jdk.incubator.foreign, in a package of the same name.
 Documentation for `jdk.incubator.foreign`
 Code for `jdk.incubator.foreign`
 OpenJ9 Support for `jdk.incubator.foreign`
OpenJ9 has its own `MethodHandle` implementation. The following is required in order to support `jdk.incubator.foreign`:
1. Implement [jdk.internal.access.JavaLangInvokeAccess]( interface (`java.lang.invoke.JavaLangInvokeAccessImpl`).
 - It gets used by [jdk.incubator.foreign.MemoryHandles]( and [jdk.internal.foreign.LayoutPath](
 - Only the following [JavaLangInvokeAccess]( methods are needed:
 JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressViewVarHandle
 JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressCarrier
 JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressByteOrder
 JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressOffset
 JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressStrides
 2. Set the implementation of `JavaLangInvokeAccess` in `SharedSecrets`:
 java.lang.System.afterClinitInitialization {
 ...
 jdk.internal.access.SharedSecrets.setJavaLangInvokeAccess(new JavaLangInvokeAccessImpl());
 ...
 }
 3. We will need to implement `java.lang.invoke.MemoryAddressViewVarHandle`. `JavaLangInvokeAccess.memoryAddressViewVarHandle` returns an instance of `MemoryAddressViewVarHandle`. `MemoryAddressViewVarHandle` should be similar to [java.lang.invoke.ByteBufferViewVarHandle](
 Deadline
Code needs to be delivered for this feature by 7th February 2020; before the next cut-off date.
 Note
There is ongoing work to consume the OpenJDK `MethodHandle` implementation in OpenJ9 (@fengxue-IS Will this work be complete by the above deadline? If yes, we can avoid all this work). This work will deprecate OpenJ9's custom implementation of `MethodHandle` and allow us to support the `jdk.incubator.foreign` package without any additional OpenJ9-specific changes. The changes proposed in this issue will need to be removed once OpenJ9 utilizes the OpenJDK `MethodHandle` implementation.

issue_title: Classes unloading threshold default is too high
description:
Classes unloading in Gencon is executed by Global GC only. So it is possible that in case if Global GC is not necessary for long period of time (Scavenge cycles handle keep heap in good shape) the large number of classes might be accumulated (not unloaded). To prevent this scenario GC might make a decision to execute Global GC instead of Local GC (percolate to Global). The real check is "If number of `Anonymous Classes loaded since last Global GC` times `Anonymous Class Weight` plus `Number of Classloaders loaded since last Global GC` exceeds Class Unloading Threshold" execute Global GC instead of Local GC.
Current default value for this threshold is set to `80000`. `Anonymous Class Weight` is set to `1.0`
Unfortunately we have a situation when time of handling of class unloading hook in JIT code might be in order of milliseconds. This leads to multi-second pauses in STW Global GC.
Looks like it is reasonable to reduce threshold to 5000 - 10000, at least temporary until slow handling of class unloading in JIT code is fixed.
Also I have a question for JIT developers: Is unloading time for Anonymous Class is smaller than average? Currently Anonymous and regular classes have equal weight but it can be changed (for example 5-10 Anonymous per regular class). The threshold was set so high to handle test case when waste amount of Anonymous classes are generated. In this case we don't want to execute Global GC too often.
@LinHu2016 @amicic @mpirvu @andrewcraik @DanHeidinga @manqingl

issue_title: Exploit cached lastITable in JIT interface dispatch
description:
I discovered that there is a `lastITable` field cached in the `J9Class` structure. Presumably, the last ITable in a class where an interface lookup was found is cached, and the next time an interface dispatch is performed on this class the interface class is compared to the latest cached interface class and if there is a match a slower lookup can be skipped.
However, only the x86 and Power JIT backends exploit this on their interface dispatches. This work was completed several years ago (circa 2015). Is this an oversight, or are there technical reasons why this wasn't exploited on Z or ARM? How much of an opportunity is there that would motivate doing the work on those platforms?
Before I add this to my list of work to be completed across all architectures (#5455) I thought I'd raise an issue.
- [ ] Z (#8399)
- [ ] AArch64 (#8400)
- [ ] ARM (#8401)
@fjeremic @knn-k @ymanton @gita-omr @andrewcraik

Is this an oversight, or are there technical reasons why this wasn't exploited on Z or ARM? How much of an opportunity is there that would motivate doing the work on those platforms?
Before I add this to my list of work to be completed across all architectures (#5455) I thought I'd raise an issue.
- [ ] Z (#8399)
- [ ] AArch64 (#8400)
- [ ] ARM (#8401)

Ie the file is readable and writeable only by `BLAH\SomeWinUser`. This user is also the owner of the file.
This causes a downstream blocker when trying to configure a pseudosecure JMX port via locked-down password and access files--in this case for Tomcat testing--in that the JVM thinks that the password file is not sufficiently restricted and immediately exits.

import sun.management.FileSystem
fs = FileSystem.open()
isAccessUserOnly = fs.isAccessUserOnly( new File( "./zzTestUserOnlyFile.txt" ) )
println "isAccessUserOnly=$isAccessUserOnly"
And for each JVM + JDK,
isAccessUserOnly=false //OpenJ9
isAccessUserOnly=true //HotSpot
isAccessUserOnly=true //Zulu HotSpot, for good measure
