issue_title: JEP 358 design and implementation notes
description:
## Overview of JEP 358: Helpful NullPointerExceptions
JEP 358 [1] provides extended messages for the NullPointerException (NPE) generated by JVM.
Current NPE comes with a non-null message supplied in a constructor or `null` particularly when it was created by the JVM. An NPE stacktrace contains the method, filename, and line number where the NPE occurred. However a single line of code may contain several access paths, each one is potentially the source of that NPE, and there is no hint about the actual offending path.
This JEP implementation aims to pinpoint the source of such NPE and identify its root cause.
## Details
 Java command-line option to enable/disable the feature
This JEP feature can be toggled with `-XX:{+|-}ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages`. It is not enabled by default at `Java 14`.
 NPE extended message description
When this feature is enabled and the JVM is about to throw an NPE, a detailed message is computed in two parts:
The first part is the consequence of this NPE, i.e., which action could not be performed because of a `null` bytecode instruction.
The second part is the reason for the NPE, i..e., which part of the source code pushed that `null` reference onto the operand stack.
An example message produced from a statement `a.b.c.i = 99` might look like following:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot read field "c" because "a.b" is null
 at Prog.main(Prog.java:5)
in which the 1st part of the NPE message is _Cannot read field "c"_, and the 2nd part is _because "a.b" is null_.
More message details accordingly to the bytecode executed:
bytecode | 1st part
-- | --
`aload` (`iaload/faload/aaload/baload/caload/saload/laload/daload`) | Cannot load from `<element type>` array
`arraylength` | Cannot read the array length
`astore` (`iastore/fastore/aastore/bastore/castore/sastore/lastore/dastore`) | Cannot store to `<element type>` array
`athrow` | Cannot throw exception
`getfield` | Cannot read field `<field name>`
`invokeinterface`, `invokespecial`, `invokevirtual` | Cannot invoke `<method>`
`monitorenter` | Cannot enter synchronized block
`monitorexit` | Cannot exit synchronized block
`putfield` | Cannot assign field `<field name>`
Any other bytecode | N/A
bytecode | 2nd part
-- | --
`aconst_null` | `null`
`aaload` | the instruction pushed the array reference followed by `[`, then the instruction pushed the index, then append `]`
`iconst_*`, `bipush`, `sipush` | the constant value
`getfield` | the instruction pushed the reference, followed by `.<field name>`
`getstatic` | `<class name>.<field name>`
`invokeinterface`, `invokevirtual`, `invokespecial`, `invokestatic` | the return value of `<method>`, or `<method>` if no first part message.
`iload*`, `aload*` | `this` for local variable `0`, the variable name if a local variable table is available, otherwise `<parameter i >` or `<local i >`.
Any other bytecode | N/A
## VM design notes
The NPE message 1st part can be determined by the bytecode being executed, the 2nd part message has to be computed based on past bytecodes already finished.
Considering the complexity work for the 2nd part message computing, VM design and implementation is going to be in two phases, first step is to provide the NPE message 1st part, then the message 2nd part. Construct NPE message 1st part The first part of extended NPE message can be computed just based on the bytecode `methodPC` where the NPE is thrown. This `methodPC` is stored at first element of `java.lang.Throwable.walkback` within current exception object by `BytecodeInterpreter.hpp:inlThrowableFillInStackTrace()` or `Fast_java_lang_Throwable_fillInStackTrace`. It can be retrieved along with the `ROM` `method`/`class` containing this `methodPC` using the algorithm in `exceptiondescribe.c:iterateStackTrace()`. To prepare the framework for the NPE part 2 message generation, a function `getCompleteNPEMessage()` is to be added within `rtverify.c`, and take advantage of `verifier` stack structure and parsing algorithm. This function performs following:
1. if the bytecode is one of `iaload/faload/aaload/baload/caload/saload/laload/daload`, `iastore/fastore/aastore/bastore/castore/sastore/lastore/dastore`, `arraylength`, `athrow`, `monitorenter`, or `monitorexit`, a specific message can be constructed accordingly just based on the bytecode itself;
2. if the bytecode is `getfield` or `putfield`, the field `name/sig` can be retrieved based on the bytecode and the field index;
3. if the bytecode is `invokeinterface`, `JBinvokeinterface2`, `invokespecial`, or `invokevirtual`, the method name can be retrieved based on the bytecode and the method index;
4. `NULL` for any other bytecodes. Computing NPE message 2nd part
To compute NPE message 2nd part, the `class`/`method`/`field` putting `null` into the stack have to be identified.
 An example
First start with an example with following code snippet:
 Object obj = new Object();
 Object[][] objsTwoDimen = new Object[2][];
 try {
 objsTwoDimen[1][3] = obj;
 } catch (NullPointerException e) {
 e.printStackTrace();
 }
A JVM w/o this JEP produces following NPE:
java.lang.NullPointerException
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.demo_aastore(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:29)
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.testAll(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:12)
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.main(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:893)
With the JEP, the NPE is expected to be:
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot store to object array because "objsTwoDimen[1]" is null
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.demo_aastore(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:29)
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.testAll(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:12)
 at a.se.java_lang_npe.MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.main(MiniNullPointerExceptionTest.java:893)
This NPE message is going to be computed when VM discovers a `null` object reference in the stack, and maps it to a message like above.
The bytecode in question is:
 0 JBnewdup 35 java/lang/Object
 3 JBdup 4 JBinvokespecial 36 java/lang/Object.<init>()V
 7 JBastore1 8 JBiconst2 9 JBanewarray 39 [Ljava/lang/Object;
 12 JBastore2 13 JBaload2 <-- loads objsTwoDimen which is not null
 14 JBiconst1 15 JBaaload <-- loads objsTwoDimen[1] which is null
 16 JBiconst3 17 JBaload1 18 JBaastore <-- NPE to be thrown
NPE is to be thrown at `18 JBaastore` due to a `null` loaded by `15 JBaaload` which loads a reference from an array, the array reference is loaded by `13 JBaload2`.
`13 JBaload2` can be used to a local variable `objsTwoDimen` or `<local2>` if the actual variable name is not available in the class file;
`14 JBiconst1 ` is the array first dimension index `1`;
`15 JBaaload` loads the array first dimension;
`16 JBiconst3` is the array second dimension index which is not need for NPE message computing;
`17 JBaload1 ` is the value to be stored which is not need either;
 stack structure similar with verifier stack
To retrieve info above for NPE message computing, an approach proposed is to create/update a stack structure similar with the verifier stack in `rtverify.c:verifyBytecodes()`.
When the NPE is thrown at `18 JBaastore`, the stack looks like:
stackTop --> [ ]
 [ <hex> ] <-- put by `17 JBaload1`
 [ <hex> ] <-- put by `16 JBiconst3`
 [ <hex> ] <-- put by `15 JBaaload`
 [ <hex> ] <-- put by `14 JBiconst1`
stackBase --> [ <hex> ] <-- put by `13 JBaload2`
Note: the value in the stack is bytecode simplified verification defines (different from those verifier type system, just enough to support stack manuniplaution), not actual bytecode.
The number and order of the top stack contents match the operand stack required by `18 JBaastore`, i.e., `..., arrayref, index, value → ...`.
Further down the stack, the number and order of the stack contents match the operand stack required by `15 JBaaload`, i.e., `..., arrayref, index → ..., value`.
At last, the local variable `objsTwoDimen` can be retrieved via `13 JBaload2` or `<local2>` if the actual variable name is not available in the class file, the array index is `1`, hence `objsTwoDimen[1]` was `null` caused NPE. Along with NPE message part 1, `Cannot store to object array because "objsTwoDimen[1]" is null` is computed.
For cases like this, all related info can be kept within the stack, however when the stack can't keep such info, another call can be started and aim for the bytecode offset putting `arrayref` onto the stack recursively until the complete info is retrieved.
 mapping the stack to bytecode
As demonstrated above example, the stack content are for stack modification purpose, and doesn't have the actual bytecode.
To keep track the bytecode putting the values to the stack, another stack structure with **same** size will be created which keeps the bytecode offset in current ROM method (there might be multiple same bytecodes hence the offset pinpoints the bytecode specified)
For the example above, the bytecode offset stack looks like:
offsetStackTop --> [ ]
 [ 17 ] --> points to `17 JBaload1`
 [ 16 ] --> points to `16 JBiconst3`
 [ 15 ] --> points to `15 JBaaload`
 [ 14 ] --> points to `14 JBiconst1`
offsetStackBase --> [ 13 ] --> points to `13 JBaload2`
These bytecode offset stack values are saved while manipulating the stack structure parsing the bytecode. implementation details
1. The stack structure parsing the bytecode is similar with verifier stack but with minimum type system to support the parsing algorithm, most of verifier utility methods (e.g. `vrfyhelp.c` & `rtverify.c`) won't be used;
2. Similarly a separated stack map structure is to be created based on the bytecode and determine the branch targets which is expected to be simpler than the verifier counterpart created by `simulateStack()` or `decompressStackMaps()`;
3. The stack is to keep earlier bytecode contents particularly for typical cases like `aaload`, when that is not possible, a recursive call is to be invoked to find the earlier stack contents which usually are POPed in verifier stack operation;
RI has inconsistent message output, will have to build testcases for those JTReg test scenarios and also those not covered by JTReg.
## Performance consideration
Performance impact is not expected when the feature is not enabled.
The performance hit with this feature enabled depends on the number of NPEs thrown by the application but should not be significant.
## Security consideration
This feature doesn't provide more source code info besides those already available in the NPE stacktrace without this feature except specific `NULL` value of individual field/method identified.
No extra security measurement is required. ## Compatibility consideration
This feature is not enabled by default, and doesn't affect existing application. There is no migration effort required. When this feature is enabled, it only affects the application/tools depending on the exact format or message of the NPE.
## Test Plan
JTReg tests [2]:
NPEInHiddenTopFrameTest.java
NullPointerExceptionTest.java
SuppressMessagesTest.java
Note: due to RI inconsistent messages and OpenJ9 doesn't match them all, JTReg tests can't be run directly.
## Documentation
A doc issue is required.
@DanHeidinga @gacholio @pshipton please comment.

description:
Hi there,
Below follows a reproduction case for a deserialization problem we have encountered in our software after an upgrade to the latest JDK (openjdk11.06 with openj9), we came from 11.05 openj9 previously. We would like to see this fixed, as we don't want to advise our customers to not use openjdk with openj9.
This occurs *only* at the 11.06 version with OpenJ9, it works fine on 11.05 with OpenJ9, it also works fine for 11.06 with hotspot.
If you have more questions please let me know. Thank you.
 JDK version
openjdk version "11.0.6" 2020-01-14
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.6+10)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.18.0, JRE 11 Mac OS X amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20200116_443 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 6968c18d7
OMR - 7a1b0239a
JCL - 104cab2452 based on jdk-11.0.6+10)
This reproduces at linux too (did not test on windows but likely as well).
 Reproduction case
Attached a simplified reproduction case using maven that reproduces the issue.
[openjdk-cl-issue.zip](
- Install maven, I used: 3.6.3
- Extract the attached .zip
- In a shell go the directory "openjdk-cl-issue", this contains the main pom.xml
- Set the JAVA_HOME environment variable: `export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/openjdk11.06-openj9` (this is what maven will use)
- `mvn clean package`
That will clean and then package and run the Main.class (present in test project). It will fail with the exception further down.
You can debug through it all as well from e.g. IntelliJ. Start from the "Main" class.
Essentially this contains 3 projects, model1, model2 and test. Both model1 and model2 are only available on compile time, so _not_ on runtime.
The Main class creates 2 separate classloaders, ClassLoaderModel1 for model1 and ClassLoaderModel2 for model2 (this one has as parent ClassLoaderModel1).
It then reflectively loads "RunTest" using ClassLoaderModel2 and calls "doIt()". In there an instance of TestData is created, serialized to byte[] and then back to TestData. It's the latter (the deserialization) that fails.
Have a look in TestData and see how it has an IdentityHashMap<String, Model1Object> where as Model1Object lives in model1 (so that ClassLoaderModel1).
During deserialization of this map, once that map is complete the ObjectInputStream's state is in:
cachedLudcl=ClassLoaderModel1
refreshLudcl=false (note: IdentityHashMap has a custom readObject()).
Then the next field is about to be serialized (simpleObject), this one lives in model2 - but since the refreshLudcl=false, it will not refresh the classloader (normally that is done by calling latestUserDefinedLoader()), causing the ClassNotFoundException as it uses the wrong classloader.
Please have a look in Model1Object and read the comment I put there, the problem is related to custom read/write serialization methods as well as another dependent object there. Without those things are working as expected.
 Additional notes
- We suspect this problem was introduced with - Disabling classcaching (as that was enabled in 11.06):
 - `MAVEN_OPTS='-Dcom.ibm.enableClassCaching=false' mvn clean package` works
- openjdk11.05 openj9 works fine with or without caching enabled (same flag, in 11.05 the default is off).
- openjdk11.06 with hotspot works fine (previous versions too).

Bug Title: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: during object deserialization in openjdk11.06 with openj9
Bug Description: Hi there,
Below follows a reproduction case for a deserialization problem we have encountered in our software after an upgrade to the latest JDK (openjdk11.06 with openj9), we came from 11.05 openj9 previously. We would like to see this fixed, as we don't want to advise our customers to not use openjdk with openj9.
This occurs *only* at the 11.06 version with OpenJ9, it works fine on 11.05 with OpenJ9, it also works fine for 11.06 with hotspot.
If you have more questions please let me know. Thank you.
 JDK version
openjdk version "11.0.6" 2020-01-14
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.6+10)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.18.0, JRE 11 Mac OS X amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20200116_443 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 6968c18d7
OMR - 7a1b0239a
JCL - 104cab2452 based on jdk-11.0.6+10)
This reproduces at linux too (did not test on windows but likely as well).
 Reproduction case
Attached a simplified reproduction case using maven that reproduces the issue.
[openjdk-cl-issue.zip](
- Install maven, I used: 3.6.3
- Extract the attached .zip
- In a shell go the directory "openjdk-cl-issue", this contains the main pom.xml
- Set the JAVA_HOME environment variable: `export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/openjdk11.06-openj9` (this is what maven will use)
- `mvn clean package`
That will clean and then package and run the Main.class (present in test project). It will fail with the exception further down.
You can debug through it all as well from e.g. IntelliJ. Start from the "Main" class.
Essentially this contains 3 projects, model1, model2 and test. Both model1 and model2 are only available on compile time, so _not_ on runtime.
The Main class creates 2 separate classloaders, ClassLoaderModel1 for model1 and ClassLoaderModel2 for model2 (this one has as parent ClassLoaderModel1).
It then reflectively loads "RunTest" using ClassLoaderModel2 and calls "doIt()". In there an instance of TestData is created, serialized to byte[] and then back to TestData. It's the latter (the deserialization) that fails.
Have a look in TestData and see how it has an IdentityHashMap<String, Model1Object> where as Model1Object lives in model1 (so that ClassLoaderModel1).
During deserialization of this map, once that map is complete the ObjectInputStream's state is in:
cachedLudcl=ClassLoaderModel1
refreshLudcl=false (note: IdentityHashMap has a custom readObject()).
Then the next field is about to be serialized (simpleObject), this one lives in model2 - but since the refreshLudcl=false, it will not refresh the classloader (normally that is done by calling latestUserDefinedLoader()), causing the ClassNotFoundException as it uses the wrong classloader.
Please have a look in Model1Object and read the comment I put there, the problem is related to custom read/write serialization methods as well as another dependent object there. Without those things are working as expected.
 Additional notes
- We suspect this problem was introduced with - Disabling classcaching (as that was enabled in 11.06):
 - `MAVEN_OPTS='-Dcom.ibm.enableClassCaching=false' mvn clean package` works
- openjdk11.05 openj9 works fine with or without caching enabled (same flag, in 11.05 the default is off).
- openjdk11.06 with hotspot works fine (previous versions too).

issue_title: Java 14 MethodHandles::privateLookupIn may not produce a Lookup with full privilege access
description:
From the Java 14 release notes
"
The Lookup object produced by MethodHandles::privateLookupIn in this release may not have full privilege access. A lookup which possesses both PRIVATE and MODULE access modes is said to possess full privilege access that can be tested with Lookup::hasFullPrivilegeAccess method. Previously a Lookup returned from MethodHandles::privateLookupIn can be used to look up caller-sensitive methods. In Java SE 14, it may fail to look up caller-sensitive methods if the lookup does not have full privilege access (even it has private access mode).
"

issue_title: J9VM_INTERP_NATIVE_SUPPORT and the corresponding flag in the Spec is outdated
description:
`J9VM_INTERP_NATIVE_SUPPORT` & the corresponding flag `interp_nativeSupport` in the existing implementation of OpenJ9 is outdated for a quite long time and doesn't work to disable JIT. Given that the flag is never used properly over years, it should be totally removed in our code to avoid any misunderstanding & misuse on this flag in the future.
FYI: @keithc-ca , @DanHeidinga, @pshipton, @gacholio.

issue_title: Using OPENJ9_JAVA_OPTIONS versus JAVA_OPTS causes confusion
description:
This issue is to discuss whether OpenJ9 should support (not ignore JAVA_OPTS), as recently there have been 3 separate users that have tried to use JAVA_OPTS and have hit difficulties. ( is one example).
JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx8000m" option is not recognized by OpenJ9, so you have to use OPENJ9_JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xmx8000m". Is this something that we can or should be addressing to minimize user confusion?

issue_title: Feature request: Allow default javacore file name for jcmd Dump.java
description:
Using jcmd with Dump.java without a filename gives an error and its help shows that a file name is required:
$ jcmd 2440 Dump.java
Error: Error in command
Error: wrong number of arguments
$ jcmd 2440 help Dump.java
Dump.java: Create a javacore file.
 Format: Dump.java <file path>
 <file path> is mandatory: there is no default.
 Relative paths are resolved to the target's working directory.
 The dump agent may choose a different file path if the requested file exists.
It would be nice if Dump.java allowed using the default (or `-Xdump`-configured) javacore name format and directory. This would be valuable because the user wouldn't have to worry about creating a unique file name (if the command is executed multiple times), allows tools that expect the default javacore file name format, avoids the user needing to know the default javacore directory to write to, and allows for easier customization of the javacore name or directory using JVM configuration.

issue_title: OpenJ9 behaves differently when SIGABRT is received by a native app
description:
## Test source code
[openj9_sigabrt_issue.zip]( [provided by @imkabir]
## Test behavior
There are two files in the testcase:
1) **test_sigabrt.c** (native app): Registers an application signal handler for `SIGABRT`. Then, it executes the Java code and sleeps.
 sigaction(SIGABRT, &shndlr, NULL);
 jenv = createJVM(&jvm);
 if(jenv == NULL)
 return 1;
 runjclass(jenv);
2) **javasample.java**: Contains the Java code.
When `SIGABRT` is sent to the native app, OpenJ9 generates the JVM core dump using JVM's `SIGABRT` handler, and the application signal handler is not invoked. On the other hand, Hotspot does not generate the JVM core dump using JVM's `SIGABRT` handler, and the application signal handler is correctly invoked. OpenJ9 needs to match Hotspot's (reference implementation's) behavior.
Refer to **readme.txt** in the attached **openj9_sigabrt_issue.zip** on how to run the test.
## CORRECT behavior using OpenJDK8-Hotspot as reference
JVM has launched
Hello, World
1.8
1.8.0_242-b08
ADD 10+20= 30
In sig handler
received SIGABRT
Killed
## WRONG OpenJDK8-OpenJ9 behavior for the above testcase
JVM has launched
Hello, World
1.8
1.8.0_242-b08
ADD 10+20= 30
JVMDUMP039I Processing dump event "abort", detail "" at 2020/03/03 - please wait.
JVMDUMP032I JVM requested System dump using '/team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/core.20200303.144436.11620.0001.dmp' in response to an event
JVMPORT030W /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern setting "|/usr/libexec/abrt-hook-ccpp %s %c %p %u %g %t e %P %I %h" specifies that the core dump is to be piped to an external program. Attempting to rename either core or core.11654.
JVMDUMP010I System dump written to /team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/core.20200303.144436.11620.0001.dmp
JVMDUMP032I JVM requested Java dump using '/team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/javacore.20200303.144436.11620.0002.txt' in response to an event
JVMDUMP010I Java dump written to /team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/javacore.20200303.144436.11620.0002.txt
JVMDUMP032I JVM requested Snap dump using '/team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/Snap.20200303.144436.11620.0003.trc' in response to an event
JVMDUMP010I Snap dump written to /team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/Snap.20200303.144436.11620.0003.trc
JVMDUMP007I JVM Requesting JIT dump using '/team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/jitdump.20200303.144436.11620.0004.dmp'
JVMDUMP010I JIT dump written to /team/babsing/projects/kabir_signal_issue/testcase/jitdump.20200303.144436.11620.0004.dmp
JVMDUMP013I Processed dump event "abort", detail "".
## Temporary FIX
Use `-Xrs:sync` (JVM option). Then, J9 won't register a signal handler for `SIGABRT`, and the application signal handler can be correctly invoked in the above testcase. It should also be noted that J9 won't register a signal handler for other signals such as `SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE, SIGTRAP and SIGABEND` when `-Xrs:sync` is specified. `-Xrs` should be used if the native application wants to completely disable JVM signal handling.

issue_title: OpenJ9 exception stack trace handling different than OpenJDK
description:
Hi all,
I have discovered a difference in behavior between OpenJ9 and OpenJDK when dealing with serializing/deserializing exceptions using the google `gson` library. Scenario
I am trying to serialize/deserialize an exception class using the Google `gson` library, and I've discovered a problem when trying to set the stack trace when running OpenJ9. My Exception class does not have a default constructor, and so when `gson` creates the class, it appears to set the value of `Throwable.enableWritableStackTrace` to false. This means that when we try to set the stack trace later on using `setStackTrace()`, the setter performs a no-op. Expected Output: Exception before serialization: com.motus.TestException
 at com.motus.Main.main(Main.java:8)
Exception after serialization: com.motus.TestException
 at com.motus.Main.main(Main.java:8)
 Actual Output: Exception before serialization: com.motus.TestException
 at com.motus.Main.main(Main.java:8)

issue_title: Runtime compressed references
description:
Runtime compressed references is a new feature which will allow a single VM to operate in compressed and non-compressed mode, as opposed to the current solution which packages two separate VMs and switches them via the redirector.
The upshot of this is that compile-time checks for compressed references are no longer allowed. This document will provide a guide for migrating to the runtime strategy.
In the old world, code like this was permissible:
#if defined(OMR_GC_COMPRESSED_POINTERS)
 code for compressed
#else
 code for full pointers
#endif
#if !defined(OMR_GC_COMPRESSED_POINTERS)
 code for full
#endif
This pattern is no longer allowed in the code, with one exception - there are structures which define fields that only appear in compressed or uncompressed builds.
In `!defined` pattern is replaced by a new flag (in order to allow for both compressed and uncompressed fields to be defined in the same build):
#if defined(OMR_GC_FULL_POINTERS)
 code for full
#endif
The "mixed mode" builds will define both `OMR_GC_COMPRESSED_POINTERS` and `OMR_GC_FULL_POINTERS`. Any code accessing optional fields must also be gated on the same option.
Performing the runtime test for compressed refs differs by component. Note that in the current single mode builds, the runtime test has no cost, as it is defined to be a compile-time true or false. The caveat is that both sides of the runtime test must be compileable whether the compressed or full flags are set.
*VM*
Replace ifdeffed code with the appropriate query of:
J9VMTHREAD_COMPRESS_OBJECT_REFERENCES(vmThread)
J9JAVAVM_COMPRESS_OBJECT_REFERENCES(javaVM)
*GC*
Replace ifdeffed code with the appropriate query of:
env->compressObjectReferences()
extensions->compressObjectReferences()
Replace pointer arithmetic and dereferences of `fj9object_t` and `fomrobject_t` with uses of the static and instance APIs on `GC_SlotObject`.
*JIT*
Replace ifdeffed code with the appropriate query of:
TR::Compiler->om.compressObjectReferences()
*DDR*
`J9BuildFlags.gc_compressedPointers` -> `J9ObjectHelper.compressObjectReferences`
`J9Object.SIZEOF` -> `J9ObjectHelper.headerSize()`
`object.clazz()` -> `J9ObjectHelper.rawClazz(object)`
`array.size()` -> `J9IndexableObjectHelper.rawSize(array)`
`J9IndexableObjectDiscontiguous.SIZEOF` -> `J9IndexableObjectHelper.discontiguousHeaderSize()`
`J9IndexableObjectContiguous.SIZEOF` -> `J9IndexableObjectHelper.contiguousHeaderSize()`
Doc issue

issue_title: jdk14 Thread.interrupt() before Thread start, after Thread stop
description:
Release notes for Java 14 contain the following.
`The specification for java.lang.Thread::interrupt allows for an implementation to only track the interrupt state for live threads, and previously this is what occurred. As of this release, the interrupt state of a Thread is always available, and if you interrupt a thread t before it is started, or after it has terminated, the query t.isInterrupted() will return true.`

issue_title: DDR should detect truncated core files
description:
extended.system testing has been failing on AIX jdk11+ for a while due to OOM problems related to setting MALLOCOPTIONS. I tried to look at some of the core files from xlinux, but all the ones I've tried show "No JRE". I also recall @dmitripivkine got a core for a crash on AIX, and had a similar problem. issue_title: JEP 331 capability available when using metronome GC, but no events are sent
description: The capability for JEP331 ( - can_generate_sampled_object_alloc_events) is available and can successfully be requested when using the metronome GC. However, not a single event is sent. According to the JVMTI spec, in such a case, the capability should (1) be not part of the available capabilites and (2) requesting that capability should result in an error, both is not the case. Alternatively, events could be sent as expected.

issue_title: Ensure vm anon classes loaded before java.base have a module set
description:
Code that should be setting the java.base module walks all the loaded classes in the `vm->systemClassLoader` which does a walk of the Class Segments processing those with the matching classloader: VM Anonymous classes - those loaded by Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass - will have a different loader in their memory segments and will be missed by that `allClassesNextDo` walk.
_Originally posted by @DanHeidinga in
creator: DanHeidinga

The assert should be guarded by `J9VM_OPT_VALHALLA_VALUE_TYPES`. FYI @tajila

issue_title: Balanced GC improvements for better utilization of fragmented memory
description:
Balanced GC is region base GC policy, in general partial garbage collector(PGC) would handle most reclaim memory, occasionally global marking phase(GMP) starts and interleaves with the PGCs, global GC and abort case in PGC should be minimum for the better performance. Logically
after GMP, JVM should have more free memory than usual, but the first PGC after GMP has more chance to get abort case(specially when region count is low, such as region count=64, there are 70% abort cases happened during the first PGC after GMP), apparently there is some free memory we can not to reuse in the case.
1, After global sweep, the memory in the regions is freed, but Balanced GC use BumpPointer memorypool for allocation, only "free tail" can be reused for GC allocation, there is no freelist to track free memory in middle of region, the region need to be compacted or collected by PGC, then the free memory can be used.
2, After GMP, the cards reference from "free memory" have not be pruned from InterRegionRememberedsets, it prevents to reuse any free memory(includes free tail) in collected regions by GMP.
creator: LinHu2016

Bug Title: Balanced GC improvements for better utilization of fragmented memory
Bug Description: Balanced GC is region base GC policy, in general partial garbage collector(PGC) would handle most reclaim memory, occasionally global marking phase(GMP) starts and interleaves with the PGCs, global GC and abort case in PGC should be minimum for the better performance. Logically
after GMP, JVM should have more free memory than usual, but the first PGC after GMP has more chance to get abort case(specially when region count is low, such as region count=64, there are 70% abort cases happened during the first PGC after GMP), apparently there is some free memory we can not to reuse in the case.
1, After global sweep, the memory in the regions is freed, but Balanced GC use BumpPointer memorypool for allocation, only "free tail" can be reused for GC allocation, there is no freelist to track free memory in middle of region, the region need to be compacted or collected by PGC, then the free memory can be used.
2, After GMP, the cards reference from "free memory" have not be pruned from InterRegionRememberedsets, it prevents to reuse any free memory(includes free tail) in collected regions by GMP.

Summary of problem
We made some changes to a class file in the Apache Ant project (DirectoryScanner.class), and let several JVMs run the corresponding test file (DirectoryScannerTest.class, has been simplified) to test that class. We found that OpenJDK 8u232, 9.0.4 and 11.0.5 can **throw the IllegalMonitorStateException and exit**, while that three versions of J9 can not detect IllegalMonitorStateException (**throw nothing**), and hang up forever when an Object instance called `wait()`. We think it is a bug in J9 implementation. When you run the class files by the steps described below, you can found a lot of output which looks like `... Executed Line: 12 ...`, those outputs indicate the current instructions JVM is running and can be used to locate the issue. By decompiling the `DirectoryScanner.class` and comparing J9's output with the decompiled code, you will find that J9 hang up exactly at `object.wait();`, which is not in a `synchronized` block. According to JVM specification, the expected behavior throws an `IllegalMonitorStateException`, but J9 did not.

1. Extract DirectoryScannerTest.zip
2. In `DirectoryScannerTest` directory, run command `java -cp sootOutput/junit-ant/:hamcrest-core-1.3.jar:junit-4.12.jar org.junit.runner.JUnitCore org.apache.tools.ant.DirectoryScannerTest`

OpenJ9 - 77c1cf708
OMR - 20db4fbc
JCL - 2a7af5674b based on jdk-11.0.5+10)
Summary of problem
We made some changes to a class file in the Apache Ant project (DirectoryScanner.class), and let several JVMs run the corresponding test file (DirectoryScannerTest.class, has been simplified) to test that class. We found that OpenJDK 8u232, 9.0.4 and 11.0.5 can **throw the IllegalMonitorStateException and exit**, while that three versions of J9 can not detect IllegalMonitorStateException (**throw nothing**), and hang up forever when an Object instance called `wait()`. We think it is a bug in J9 implementation. When you run the class files by the steps described below, you can found a lot of output which looks like `... Executed Line: 12 ...`, those outputs indicate the current instructions JVM is running and can be used to locate the issue. By decompiling the `DirectoryScanner.class` and comparing J9's output with the decompiled code, you will find that J9 hang up exactly at `object.wait();`, which is not in a `synchronized` block. According to JVM specification, the expected behavior throws an `IllegalMonitorStateException`, but J9 did not.

[DirectoryScannerTest.zip](
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Extract DirectoryScannerTest.zip
2. In `DirectoryScannerTest` directory, run command `java -cp sootOutput/junit-ant/:hamcrest-core-1.3.jar:junit-4.12.jar org.junit.runner.JUnitCore org.apache.tools.ant.DirectoryScannerTest`

issue_title: ExtendedMemoryMXBeanImpl can cause a ClassLoader leak
description:
com.ibm.lang.management.internal.ExtendedMemoryMXBeanImpl can cause an application ClassLoader to leak when an application is stopped and the ClassLoader is allowed to garbage collect. The leak comes when addNotificationListener is called on a Thread whose context ClassLoader is set to an application ClassLoader. When that ClassLoader is allowed to garbage collect, it will be kept in memory by the MemoryNotificationThread that is started when addNotificationListener is called. This happens because MemoryNotificationThread inherits the ClassLoader of the Thread that started it.
To resolve this issue, I can come up with two solutions:
1. Update the context ClassLoader of the Thread when it is created to be the ExtendedMemoryMXBeanImpl.class.getClassLoader()
2. Update the Class to have a Thread field that is created during class initialization, i.e. private final Thread notifier = new MemoryNotificationThread(this);
My preference is #1 since #2 doesn't guarantee that the Class is not loaded by a Thread that doesn't have an application ClassLoader as its context ClassLoader. So if that is the case, then you would need to do #1 potentially as well in the constructor.

issue_title: Improve tracing options for jitdump scenarios
description:
The optimizer has a neat API called `traceOptimization` [1] which is used in the options table (example in [2]) to set a bit in a bitvector corresponding to the optimization ID. This mechanism is used later to test the bitvector to determine if a specific optimization will be traced.
Before the start of each optimization the optimization ID is encoded into the VM state value, such that if we crash during an optimization we can decode the optimization ID during the jitdump process and enable tracing of the failing opt. using the optimization ID and the `traceOptimization` API.
This is a great concept, however today it does not apply to all tracing that can be enabled. For example we completely lack this notion for codegen phases and certain types of more fine grained tracing. Some tracing also seems to be unused and can be eliminated.

Bug Title: Improve tracing options for jitdump scenarios
Bug Description: The optimizer has a neat API called `traceOptimization` [1] which is used in the options table (example in [2]) to set a bit in a bitvector corresponding to the optimization ID. This mechanism is used later to test the bitvector to determine if a specific optimization will be traced.
Before the start of each optimization the optimization ID is encoded into the VM state value, such that if we crash during an optimization we can decode the optimization ID during the jitdump process and enable tracing of the failing opt. using the optimization ID and the `traceOptimization` API.
This is a great concept, however today it does not apply to all tracing that can be enabled. For example we completely lack this notion for codegen phases and certain types of more fine grained tracing. Some tracing also seems to be unused and can be eliminated.

Summary of problem
My JNI program accidentally passed non-UTF8 characters when it calls _GetStaticMethodID_ method. For example, consider below code:
jclass jcl = (*env)->FindClass(env, "Class1");
char *name = calloc(100, sizeof(char));
strcat(name, "private");
strcat(name, "Static");
strcat(name, TYPE_NAME[-1]); //problem here
strcat(name, "Method1");
(*env)->GetStaticMethodID(env,jcl,name,"(I)V"); //name consists of non-utf8 chars
The above program triggers an assertion failure on OpenJ9 (build 12.0.2+10), and program terminates.
However, the same program does not terminate (infinite loop) on OpenJ9 (build 11.0.6+10, and build 1.8.0_242-b08), and no error message is shown on these versions.
It seems that assertion checks are missing on OpenJ9 (build 1.8.0_242-b08 and build 11.0.6+10) which leads to infinite loop.

issue_title: UNB network issues are preventing nightly testing
description:
This also affects testing during the day. Although it mostly works because of the reduced load, it's quite a bit slower to test on the UNB platforms.
Since the night of May 12th, we're not getting nightly coverage of the platforms tested at UNB: xlinux, mac, most plinux. The problems appear to be network related, related to github.com. I've included some stats below that @AdamBrousseau collected.
- Transfer speeds on git fetch around 20KiB/s
- Affecting all UNB machines (x/p/osx) (OpenJ9 & OMR)
- Can pull Adopt binaries fine (Backed by amazonaws) 4MB/s
- Started Tuesday May 12 (Looking at OMR farm)
 - Last good build May 11 7:33pm
 - First bad build May 12 12:22pm (Still passed)
 - Even worse by 5:03pm (Timed out git clone after 10 minutes)

x

- Bad May 12 11:57am (18.5min for the same clones)

- Bad May 12 11:57am - 19min
- Ugly May 13 2:37pm - 1 hour
osx
- Good May 11 6:06pm - 5min
- Bad May 12 11:57am - 18min

issue_title: Fix incorrect tests for mtvsr* instruction support
description: As discovered while refactoring the `TR::CPU` class in it seems that there exist several locations in the code that were performing `== TR_PPCp8` tests instead of `>= TR_PPCp8` tests when trying to detect support for the POWER8 `mtvsrd` and `mtvsrwz` instructions. This results in these instructions being detected as unavailable on POWER9 machines, causing the fallback path to use a load/store sequence instead. These faulty tests should be changed so that these instructions are used on POWER9.
creator: aviansie-ben
text:
Bug Title: Fix incorrect tests for mtvsr* instruction support
Bug Description: As discovered while refactoring the `TR::CPU` class in it seems that there exist several locations in the code that were performing `== TR_PPCp8` tests instead of `>= TR_PPCp8` tests when trying to detect support for the POWER8 `mtvsrd` and `mtvsrwz` instructions. This results in these instructions being detected as unavailable on POWER9 machines, causing the fallback path to use a load/store sequence instead. These faulty tests should be changed so that these instructions are used on POWER9.

issue_title: jdk8 ProcessorMXBean is not a properly installed MXBean
description:
As we are getting closer to publishing javadoc ( which will include it, we should consider what to do about com.ibm.lang.management.ProcessorMXBean. Probably just delete the code.
This is not a properly installed MXBean, it's not included in com.ibm.java.lang.management.internal.ManagementUtils. This class is available in jdk8 only, excluded in higher versions. The implementation was never approved as something the project wanted to support, and the implementation was never completed.
The code is directly callable via `new com.ibm.lang.management.internal.ProcessorMXBeanImpl()`, but otherwise I don't think it can be used. It provides the following APIs:
getNumberPhysicalCPUs()
getNumberOnlineCPUs()
getNumberBoundCPUs()
getNumberTargetCPUs()
setNumberActiveCPUs()

issue_title: Windows 32 bit version is not built Large address aware
description:
Duplicated from - Platform and architecture (e.g. Linux/x64:
Windows W32

Both jdk8u252-b09 jdk8u232-b09
- Variant e.g. HotSpot or OpenJ9:
OpenJ9
- Have you tested it with other vendors' java:
Yes IBM version is Large address aware
- Steps to reproduce:
dumpbin /headers java.exe |grep -i large
or
dumpbin /headers nlnotes.exe |grep -i large
If nothing found can't handle >2GB address

The openJDK J9 32 bit version is not built Large address aware and therefore cannot address memory > 2 GB and so the command fails. The headers output does not have this line in it:
`Application can handle large (>2GB) addresses`
dumpbin /headers nlnotes.exe |grep -i large
or
dumpbin /headers java.exe |grep -i large

description:
> It would be good to confirm in case we decide to go with this option.
For existing OpenJ9 `System.mapLibraryName(userLibName)` returning `.so`, I tested `ClassLoaderHelper.mapAlternativeName()` patch as following at 1. rename `libnio.so` to `libnio.a`;
2. `-version` failed with `UnsatisfiedLinkError`;
3. `-version` succeeds with the patch `ClassLoaderHelper.mapAlternativeName()` which returns `.a`.
Building a JDK15 AIX to verify that the similar patch (returning `.so`) also works when `System.mapLibraryName(userLibName)` returning `.a`.
**Update:**
Verified that `JDK15 AIX` still builds with `System.mapLibraryName(userLibName)` returning `.a` like `JDK 8 & 11`, and adding `aix/classes/jdk/internal/loader/ClassLoaderHelper.java` in which `mapAlternativeName()` returns `.so`.

description:

`SH_OSCache::generateCacheUniqueID()` is called twice: the first time with a `NULL` buffer (to determine the amount of space required) and a second time with a buffer which is of a size determined by the first call. Part of the computation involves the length of a file (see [line 1399]( It's entirely reasonable that another process using the same cache has increased the size of the file between those two calls, with the result that the second call fails with the assertion shown above.

issue_title: Track JDK commits which need OpenJDK MethodHandle support
description: In JDK15+, commits dependent on the OpenJDK MethodHandle(s) were noticed. These commits cannot be supported with the OpenJ9 MethodHandle implementation. These commits are temporarily reverted (disabled) until OpenJ9 supports the OpenJDK MethodHandle(s). This issue will track all such commits so that their revert can be undone once OpenJ9 supports the OpenJDK MethodHandles(s).

issue_title: Spec clarification: Final fields in records are not reflectively modifiable
description:
OpenJDK has clarified the specification for reflection to state that "Final fields in records are not reflectively modifiable" [0]
We need to validate the OpenJ9 applies this constraint on reflection correctly and Unsafe. MethodHandles and VarHandles already disallow setting final fields, though there may be a `setAccessible` path through MethodHandles.unreflect() that allows it - need some testing to confirm.
This inability to reflectively write final fields also applies to JDK 15 hidden classes, to Records, and to static final fields in all classes and interfaces.
[0]

issue_title: ValueTypes: revisit valuetype pre-padding
description:
We had to introduce the concept of pre-padding for for standalone VTs to satisfy alignment constraints. We need to do this for instance fields on compressedRefs because VTs do not have lockwords so fields always begin on a 4byte boundary.
The offset is calculated from the object header. So in compressedrefs backfill == 0 means offset 4 from the start of the object, backfill == 4 means offset 8 from the start of the object.
For arrays however since the header is always going to be a multiple of U_64 and the stride length is always going to be correctly aligned, the backfill offset is not needed and the array elements can always be written at "backfill 0". Similarly, for flattened instance fields backfill is essentially zero since we dont want gaps between fields.
When the VT is flattened in an instance field we ignore (subtract) the pre-padding so there are no gaps in the instance layout. This was not done for array elements which led to bugs, and The proposed solution is to modify the array scanner to detect this, in the future we may want to come up with a better solution.

Bug Description: We had to introduce the concept of pre-padding for for standalone VTs to satisfy alignment constraints. We need to do this for instance fields on compressedRefs because VTs do not have lockwords so fields always begin on a 4byte boundary.
The offset is calculated from the object header. So in compressedrefs backfill == 0 means offset 4 from the start of the object, backfill == 4 means offset 8 from the start of the object.
For arrays however since the header is always going to be a multiple of U_64 and the stride length is always going to be correctly aligned, the backfill offset is not needed and the array elements can always be written at "backfill 0". Similarly, for flattened instance fields backfill is essentially zero since we dont want gaps between fields.
When the VT is flattened in an instance field we ignore (subtract) the pre-padding so there are no gaps in the instance layout. This was not done for array elements which led to bugs, and The proposed solution is to modify the array scanner to detect this, in the future we may want to come up with a better solution.

issue_title: Replacing master/slave with more inclusive terms
description:
Due to recent events and in alignment with IBM's emb(race) pledge the IBM style guide has recently flagged certain words as "do not use" list for public content such as:
Instead of using: blacklist & whitelist
use: blocklist & allowlist
Instead of using: master & slave
use:
- coordinator/controller/leader/main/manager/parent/primary
- worker/child/helper/replica/secondary
Since OpenJ9 feeds into IBM J9 I think it makes sense to adopt this language here as well.
I noticed that the terminology master/slave threads are used quite a bit in gc code. I'm happy to make the changes for this but can someone more familiar with that area advise on what words make the most sense to use as alternates?

issue_title: Containerized JVM will not use more than 25GB heap without explicit configuration
description:
Java -version output
$ java -version
openjdk version "11.0.8" 2020-07-14
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.8+10)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.21.0, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20200715_697 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 34cf4c075
OMR - 113e54219
JCL - 95bb504fbb based on jdk-11.0.8+10)
Summary of problem
When running an OpenJ9 JVM in a container that is given a memory limit of 40gb or higher, the JVM never auto-detects more than 25gb of usable max heap. According to the documentation for the "UseContainerSupport" flag, we were expecting to see the JVM use up to 75% of the available memory limit as heap.
More specifically:
- With no explicit -Xms or -Xmx or any other memory-sizing options set, the JVM would correctly auto-set the max heap to 75% of the memory limit — but only up to a point.
- That point seemed to be a hard limit of 25gb for max heap. After that point, it didn’t seem to matter how high I set the memory limit to, the JVM would never set the max heap higher than 25 gb. We would see JVM startup output verifying that the limit was recognized, but that the heap was still limited to 25gb, e.g.:
Operating System Metrics:
...
 Memory Limit: 40.00G
 Memory Soft Limit: Unlimited
 Memory & Swap Limit: 40.00G
 Kernel Memory Limit: Unlimited
 TCP Memory Limit: Unlimited
 Out Of Memory Killer Enabled: true
...
VM settings:
 Min. Heap Size: 16.00M
 Max. Heap Size (Estimated): 25.00G
 Using VM: Eclipse OpenJ9 VM
- When I explicitly set MaxRAMPercentage (to 75 in this case), the JVM will set the max heap according to the memory limit and would go beyond 25gb. Again, up until a certain point where the compressed refs boundary of 63.75gb was hit.

issue_title: Missing checks on class descriptor when Xcheck:jni is enabled
description:
Java -version output
openjdk version "11.0.6" 2020-01-14
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.6+10)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.18.1, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20200122_441 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 51a5857
OMR - 7a1b0239a
JCL - da35e0c380 based on jdk-11.0.6+10)
Summary of problem
It seems that OpenJ9's Xcheck:jni does not check class descriptor as incorrect descriptor is successfully passed to FindClass JNI function. Consider below code:
(*env)->FindClass(env, "Ljava/lang/Object;");
"Ljava/lang/Object;" is incorrect class descriptor as JNI specification stated as follow:
For example, the fully-qualified class name for the java.lang.String class is:
 "java/lang/String"
reference : Hotspot 11 correctly detects incorrect class descriptor. Hotspot 11 shows below error message.
WARNING in native method: JNI FindClass received a bad class descriptor "Ljava/lang/Object;". A correct class descriptor has no leading "L" or trailing ";". Incorrect descriptors will not be accepted in future releases.
However, OpenJ9 accepts incorrect class descriptor and does not throw error message.
Diagnostic files
[test8.zip](

issue_title: JEP 358 NullPointerException messages enabled by default for jdk 15
description:
From OpenJDK 15 release notes.
"
Enable ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages by default (JDK-8233014)
hotspot/runtime
The default of the flag ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages was changed to 'true'. The helpful NullPointerException messages of JEP 358 are now printed by default. The messages contain snippets of the code where the NullPointerException was raised.
App deployers should double check the output of their web applications and similar usage scenarios. The NullPointerException message could be included in application error messages or be displayed by other means in the app. This could give remote attackers valuable hints about a potential vulnerable state of the software components being used.
An example message is 'Cannot read field "c" because "a.b" is null'. The attacker knows that field b of a contains null which might be unintended and offer an opportunity for an attack. For more details of what the message can contain see above mentioned JEP 358.
"

issue_title: Proposal to remove ARM32 support from OpenJ9
description:
I would like to propose removing support for the 32-bit ARM processor from OpenJ9.
This support was contributed when OpenJ9 was first open sourced in 2017 but there has been no significant community interest in it, no builds or binaries produced at AdoptOpenJDK, and a lack of support for Java features introduced since JDK 8. The code paths remain largely untested, with only the occasional JDK 8 cross-compile build occurring internally within IBM (i.e., no tests, only builds).
Granted, there has been some limited grassroots interest in running OpenJ9 on older Raspberry Pis and similar embedded devices, but in my opinion not enough to justify the human and hardware resource cost of modernizing, building, and maintaining it.
Removing 32-bit ARM code from OpenJ9 will eliminate this technical debt and simplify some code paths. The code will remain in the GitHub repo should someone decide in the future to resurrect it and provide resources to modernize, build, test, and maintain it. In practical terms, the bulk of this support is in the JIT, the JIT runtime, VM-JIT glue, and build infrastructure.
Note that this proposal only applies to OpenJ9. It does not propose removing the 32-bit ARM code generator support from the OMR project which could still be useful in some language environments on some devices.
Input from the community is welcome on this proposal (please comment below). If there are appeals for clemency I'm particularly interested in the use cases. My goal is to make a decision on its disposition by Sept 4.

issue_title: ValueTypes: Warnings for ValueBased Classes (JEP 390)
description:
See ValueTypes: Warnings for ValueBased Classes (JEP 390)
A new annotation `@ValueBased` will be introduced and applied to classes that may become inline-types in the future. Inline-types disallow synchronization on instances. To facilitate migration of `@ValueBased` classes to inline-types, the RI will add an option to fail, warn, or emit a JFR event when a monitor enter occurs on an instance of a `@ValueBased` class. This option will not be turned on by default.
For more info on value based classes see: The `@ValueBased` annotation may be applied to the following classes:
- The primitive wrapper classes in java.lang: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Boolean, and Character
- The "optional" classes in java.util: Optional, OptionalInt, OptionalLong, and OptionalDouble
- Many classes in the java.time API: Instant, LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, ZoneId, OffsetTime, OffsetDateTime, ZoneOffset, Duration, Period, Year, YearMonth, and MonthDay; and, in java.time.chrono, MinguoDate, HijrahDate, JapaneseDate, and ThaiBuddhistDate
- The value-based classes in the jdk.incubator.foreign module
- and more
Openj9 can implement a similar option to warn or fail when a monitor enter occurs on an instance of a `@ValueBased` class. An exception `VirtualMachineError` can be thrown on monitor enter in the case of fail. And a warning message can be printed if the warn is specified. Overview:
1) @ValueBased will be detected when building the romClass just like @Contended, etc.
 - I believe the full name is jdk.internal.ValueBased (will need to confirm this)
2) A flag will be added to the ramClass J9ClassIsValueBased
3) Add J9VM flags to denote whether an exception will be thrown or an error message will be outputted.
 - J9_EXTENDED_RUNTIME2_VALUE_BASED_WARNING
 - J9_EXTENDED_RUNTIME2_VALUE_BASED_EXCEPTION
 Also add an internalVMFunction helper `BOOLEAN areValueBasedMonitorChecksEnabled()` (this will be called by the JIT). It will return true if either flag is set.
4) Update the locking code (monitorEnter, jitmonitor in cnathelp, etc. see to figure out all the places to change) to detect a mask `(J9ClassIsValueType | J9ClassIsValueBased)` instead of just `J9ClassIsValueType`
5) In the exception path determine which kind of failure it is and throw the appropriate exception
6) Add cmdline option `-XX:addValueBasedClassChecks=[exception|warn]` (name is subject to change)
 This will set the flags in section 3) at VM startup.

issue_title: Optional workaround for jextract RAS build id difference when processing core file
description:
There was a crash on plinux in the builds last night ( something we've been chasing. I want to jextract the core file and get the system libraries so we can look at it (the crashing machine doesn't have gdb installed). The builds last night don't contain the latest jextract fix when I tried to use a build containing the fix, I got the following error.
java.lang.Error: J9RAS.buildID is incorrect (found <hex>, expecting <hex>). This version of jextract is incompatible with this dump.
 at com.ibm.jvm.j9.dump.extract.Main.getEnvironmentPointer(Native Method)
 at com.ibm.jvm.j9.dump.extract.Main.<init>(Main.java:469)
 at com.ibm.jvm.j9.dump.extract.Main.main(Main.java:342)
Error. Unable to locate executable for core.20200923.055935.1753.0001.dmp
I think there is no reason a different buildID can't be used to process the core file and collect the system libraries. Discussing with Keith on slack, he suggested this is advanced behavior, as it could end up collecting the wrong set of shared libraries for the jvm if the original jvm has been replaced at the same location. We can still have a workaround to disable the check, in the form of a system properly like `jextract -J-Djextract.disable.J9RAS.buildID.check <core>` to be used by advanced users only. Keith suggested printing a warning is appropriate when using this option, which I agree with.

issue_title: Snapshot and Restore application state
description:
Persist Application state
This is a large PR and consists of many different changes, they are
described below:
Persist portlibrary in image file
Even with ASLR disabled shared libs files can be mapped into different
memory addresses from run to run. This can happen if there are
differences (difference from snapshot to restore run) in the way java
launcher (java.c) allocates memory before it calls createJavaVM. Any
difference can cause the libj9vm.so to be loaded at a different address.
I have been able to observe this consistently by simply varying the
length of cmdline args (which is necessary since snapshot args will be
longer than restore).
The problem with shared libs moving around is that there are persisted
structures which have pointers to code, if the address of code changes
then these pointers need to be updated.
This PR specifically addresses the cases where structures (such as
hashtables) have direct references to the portlib which has pointer to
code. This PR persists the portlib so that on a restore run only the
portlib has to be fixed up and not all the places that referred to it.
This PR also removes the MAP_FIXED arg to mmap and verifies that the
mapped address is what is expected, if not JVM startup fails. I am yet
to observe a startup failure due to this with ASLR turned off.
Snapshot Trigger
Snapshots snapshot creation occurs while the application is running.
Snapshots can be triggered by providing the commandline arg below:
-Xsnapshot:file=[imageName],trigger=[className].[methodName]
The `imageName` specifies the name of the file which will containe the
snapshot image. The `,trigger` with the `className` and `methodName`
specifies the method which will trigger the snapshot. The snapshot is
triggered on method entry. The trigger clause is currently a requirement
to create a snapshot, in the future we can pick a suitable default and
not make it a requirement.
Example
`-Xsnapshot:file=image,trigger=Hello.snapshot`
`-Xrestore:file=image`
Internally, the triggering mechanism works by making use of the vmhook
mechanism (this is also what the method trace engine uses). The JVM will
parse the options and register a classload hook to find the trigger
method when its loaded. When the method is found the JVM will register a
method entry hook and call the snapshot code once the method is entered.
Application State snapshot/restore
When a snapshot is triggered the following steps occur:
1) JVM will acquire exclusive access on the thread that triggered the
snapshot.
2) GC hook enter snapshot mode is called
3) GC hook registerGCForSnapshot is called
4) The JVM will save the required J9JavaVM structures, like jitconfig
(not really necessary) the portlibrary (important) and the vm struct in
the snapshot header (very important) so it can be found again on the
restore.
5) PreWriteToImage hook:
- pop special stack frame (this is the frame built for method hook
events) and push an internalnativestack frame (we need this to allocat
jni localrefs on the initjavavm phase in the restore) and save bp in
`tempSlot`.
- detach VMthread from OMr
- detach javaVM from OMR
- unresolve all native methods (inls, jni, etc)
- null out custom spin options (will be repopulated on restore)
6) Write image to file - same as before
- this is that state that will be restored
7) PostWriteToImage hooks
- attach javaVM to omr
- attach thread to OMR
- pop nativeinternal stack frame
- push special frame
8) Call GC leaveSnapshotMode hook
9) Release exclusive VM access
When a snapshot is restored the following steps occur:
1) Read image from file and re-init snapshotimple monitors -- same as
before
2) Restore J9JavaVM structures
- Null out state that couldnt be persisted (zip cache, mgmfuncs,
deadthread list, sharedcache API, etc.)
- memset omrVM and omrRuntime structs
3) Restore classloaders
- reset all native lib handles
- reset jniRedirection blocks
- reset gclinks (maybe not required)
- reset zip file handle in cpentries
4) Re-init memory segment monitors
5) Restore portlib, fixup all portlib functions pointers
- this could be a relocation but not really worth doing that since
portlib functions are always called indirectly so its easier and more
efficient to just update the table.
6) init invalid itables - same as before
- shoud revisit this, may not be needed any more
7) Restore thread that triggered snapshot as main thread
- this is why only single threaded apps are supported right now
8) Run modified javaVM initstage
- All init stages are run normally except JCL init, a modified version
is run which doesnt call the class lib init code, see
`restoreRunStandardInit`.
9) Intercept call to main function from java launcher and restore thread
instead
Limitations
- single threaded
- interpreter only
- -Xms needs to be 1m larger on restore
- unsafe.realloc isnot supported (currently not used by the jcl)
- only java8 is supported
- only optthruput gc is supported
Life Cycle API (SnapshotControl)
This API allows a user to register hooks that will run before a snapshot
is created (registerPreSnapshotHooks) and hooks that will run
immediately after the snapshot is restored before re-entering the
application. This API will also allow users to programmatically create
snapshots. Currently, only `registerPostRestoreHooks` are supported.
The snapshot hooks are essentially wrappers around `Runnable` objects.
The hooks have a priority asoociated with default (low, med, high). The
priority will determine which order the hooks are run in. Default
priority is med.
Restoring JCL
The fundamental challenge with this snapshot/restore approach is that
the JVM has very little control over the state that belongs to the OS
(ie. file handles, native threads, sockets, static memory, etc.). In
many of these cases the JVM cannot persist that state, it must recreate
it on the restore run.
In the JCL there are any classes that stash JNImethod/fieldIDs in static
memory which the JVM knows nothing about. This static memory is
initialized during the static init of the class. Since the static init
of the class will not be re-run on the restore run (re-running them
could potentially mutate the application state), the functions that set
up the JNI ids must be explicitly run before the application is
restored. The list of classes that are affected by this are in
`listOfClassesThatRequireJNIIDInit`. These are run with post restore
hooks on med priority.
Similarly, there are native lib that the JCL requires. These libs are
open y the JVM with `dlopen` in the snapshot run. The JVM must re-open
them on the restore run so resolve native methods can be found again.
Post restore hooks are used to re-load the native libs. These hooks are
high priority as some of the libraries are need very early in the JVM
lifecycle.
Example
On ubuntu18,
Demo app
public class Hello {
 static double d = Math.random();
 static void snapshot() {}
 public static void main(String args[]) throws Throwable {
 System.out.print("Do bunch of init .");
 Thread.sleep(1500);
 System.out.print(" .");
 Thread.sleep(1500);
 System.out.print(" .");
 Thread.sleep(1500);
 System.out.print(" .");
 Thread.sleep(1500);
 System.out.println("\n finished init");
 snapshot();//< snapshot here
 System.out.println("Starting receiving requests");
 }
}
turn off ASLR:
`setarch `uname -m` -R /bin/bash`
get demo.jar from [redacted] - you can use example code to build it
create snapshot: `./java -Xint -Xmx16m -Xms8m -Xgcpolicy:optthruput
-Xshare:off -Xsnapshot:file=image,trigger=Hello.snapshot -cp ~/. Hello`
restore snapshot: `./java -Xint -Xmx16m -Xms9m -Xgcpolicy:optthruput
-Xshare:off -Xrestore:file=image -cp ~/. Hello`
Let me know if there are any issues

issue_title: jcmd doesn't request system dumps with exclusive access
description: jcmd requests system dumps without options, which means it defaults to without exclusive access. This can make the dumps unusable. The `Dump.system` option already takes a filename parameter. The command can be extended to take other parameters as well so the user can set any options. It may be worth making the default parameters `request=exclusive+prepwalk` if nothing is specified.

issue_title: OpenJ9 -Xlog is a different option than Hotspot -Xlog
description:
Hotspot introduced JEP 158 (see which adds the -Xlog option. OpenJ9 already implements a -Xlog option for a different purpose When the Hotspot -Xlog is used with OpenJ9 it causes a `JVMJ9VM085W Malformed option:` error.
OpenJ9 now parses the JAVA_OPTIONS environment variable for compatibility, which may contain Hotspot options. This may cause problems when JAVA_OPTIONS contains options which are not compatible with OpenJ9.
What I suggest is - add an alternative form of the OpenJ9 `-Xlog:` option, such as `-XOSLog:`, and deprecate the existing `-Xlog:` option.
- introduce another option like `-XX:-LegacyXlogOption`, which could become default for OpenJ9 builds. It would stop processing of the OpenJ9 `-Xlog:` option. - when `-XX:-LegacyXlogOption` is enabled, add processing for the Hotspot `-Xlog` option. The simplest form of this is to ignore the option, or print a warning that `-Xlog` isn't a valid OpenJ9 option. More complicated processing could map forms of `-Xlog` to options that OpenJ9 understands, such as `-Xlog:gc` to `-verbose:gc`, and understanding the `file=` suboption as well in order to set ` -Xverbosegclog`.

issue_title: jvm_compiler_0 test got 329 failures with openj9
description:
Failure link
- Grinder Link: - test category: extended.openjdk
- test target name: jvm_compiler_0
- OS/architecture: openjdk_x86-64_linux
The failed tests can mainly be classified into following reasons:
- aot failure, because openj9 does not provide aot material, e.g. [compiler/aot/DeoptimizationTest.java.DeoptimizationTest](
- UnsatisfiedLinkError, when file does not exist in native folder, e.g. [TestFloatJNIArgs](
- VM option does not exist, e.g. [TestSplitIfUnswitchedLoopsEliminated](
- invalid boolean value: `null' for expression `vm.xxx’, e.g. [rtm/cli/TestRTMAbortThresholdOption](
- Compilation failed, e.g. [compilercontrol/parser/DirectiveParserTest](
- RuntimeException: Expected to get exit value of X, e.g. [arguments/CheckCICompilerCount](
- missing from stdout/stderr, e.g. [c2/Test6857159](
Related to issue: eclipse/openj9#10757

issue_title: Cache well-known class chain offsets in JITServer client session
description: Every AOT compilation using SVM at the JITServer sends a SharedCache_storeSharedData message to the client in SymbolValidationManager::populateWellKnownClasses(). Most of these calls return a pointer to the same existing version of well-known class chain offsets in the client's SCC (after all well-known classes are loaded, which normally happens early on during start-up). To avoid these repeated messages, we can cache the pointers to well-known class chain offsets in the ClientSession.
creator: AlexeyKhrabrov

issue_title: ValueTypes: Field flattening issue on noncompressedRefs
description:
With full pointers mode the GC barriers use U_64 size loads/stores to copy flattened fields. Nested fields have a U_32 sized granularity, this causes an issue with the barriers in full pointers mode as when the barriers perform the copyfields operation it may perform a load/store that spans two different nested types.
To solve this we need to ensure that on full pointers mode, nested fields are padded to a U_64 granularity if there is going to be a field following it. This change needs to be made in `ObjectFieldInfo::countInstanceFields` and `resolvefield::fieldOffsetsFindNext`
`resolvefield::fieldOffsetsFindNext` will be simpler as it is possible to determine the preceding field since it keeps track of the current offset. `ObjectFieldInfo::countInstanceFields` will need to be modified in a similar manner.
creator: tajila
text:
Bug Title: ValueTypes: Field flattening issue on noncompressedRefs
Bug Description: With full pointers mode the GC barriers use U_64 size loads/stores to copy flattened fields. Nested fields have a U_32 sized granularity, this causes an issue with the barriers in full pointers mode as when the barriers perform the copyfields operation it may perform a load/store that spans two different nested types.
To solve this we need to ensure that on full pointers mode, nested fields are padded to a U_64 granularity if there is going to be a field following it. This change needs to be made in `ObjectFieldInfo::countInstanceFields` and `resolvefield::fieldOffsetsFindNext`
`resolvefield::fieldOffsetsFindNext` will be simpler as it is possible to determine the preceding field since it keeps track of the current offset. `ObjectFieldInfo::countInstanceFields` will need to be modified in a similar manner.

issue_title: cmdlinetester waits forever when killing child process doesn't work
description:
Adopt is experiencing hangs running tests using the cmdlinetester when the child process hangs and cannot be killed. The cmdlinetester waits forever for the child process.
Copied from The failure on jdk8 Windows is likely to be because the ProcessKiller logic failed to kill the process, Windows processes can be stubborn at being killed, we are seeing many orphaned testcase Processes in Windows. We are looking at adding some post-testcase Process cleanup to avoid this.
It would be beneificial though in this situation if the proc.waitFor() did not wait forever for it to finish, as it won't! So maybe some arbitrary 30 minutes timeout or something?
As it stands it is causing the whole build pipeline to hang all night.....!

issue_title: Panama: name conflict with IBM jextract and OpenJDK jextract
description:
As part of project Panama, Oracle will be releasing an application called jextract
jextract is a simple - but convenient - tool which generates a Java API from one or more native C headers. The tool can be obtained by building the foreign-jextract branch of Panama foreign repository.
Interacting with the jextract tool usually involves two steps:
 Use the jextract tool to generate a java interface for some C header files
 Write a Java program which invokes the wrapper API points generated by jextract
The jextract tool provides some basic options in order to control how the extraction process works; these are listed below:
 -C <String> - specify arguments to be passed to the underlying Clang parser
 -I <String> - specify include files path
 -l <String> - specify a library (name or full absolute path) which should be linked when the generated API is loaded
 -d <String> - specify where to place generated files
 -t <String> specify the target package for the generated classes
 --filter <String> - simple string-based filtering mechanism; only symbols from headers whose absolute path contains the specified string will be included in the generated API
 --source - generate java sources instead of classfiles
The remainder of this documents shows some basic usage examples of the jextract tool.
IBM JDKs have an application called jextract:
Use the jextract utility to process system dumps.
For an analysis of core dumps from Linux and AIX® platforms, copies of executable files and libraries are required along with the system dump. You must run the jextract utility provided in the SDK to collect these files. You must run jextract using the same SDK level, on the same system that produced the system dump. The jextract utility compresses the dump, executable files, and libraries into a single .zip file for use in subsequent problem diagnosis.
When a core file is generated, run the jextract utility against the core file with the following syntax:
jextract <core file name> [<zip_file>]
Copy code
to generate a compressed file in the current directory, containing the dump and the required executable file and libraries. The jextract utility is in the directory sdk/jre/bin. If you run jextract on a JVM level that is different from the one on which the dump was produced you see the following messages:
J9RAS.buildID is incorrect (found <hex>, expecting <hex>). This version of jextract is incompatible with this dump. Failure detected during jextract, see previous message(s).

issue_title: Remove J9VM_JIT_NEW_INSTANCE_PROTOTYPE macro
description:
Remove uses of the `J9VM_JIT_NEW_INSTANCE_PROTOTYPE` macro and fold associated code guarded with it assuming it is always **defined**.
Original question:
> If memory serves, `J9VM_JIT_NEW_INSTANCE_PROTOTYPE` guards the newInstanceImpl work that was completed literally 20 years ago. Is there any reason to keep guarding it, or should we assume it is always on by default? Have we ever disabled it for some reason?
>
>My understanding is that there are several places in the JIT where this is assumed enabled (and hence unguarded), so disabling `J9VM_JIT_NEW_INSTANCE_PROTOTYPE` will likely cause problems.
>
>Opinions? @gacholio

issue_title: Add aviansie-ben to Jenkins whitelist
description:
@aviansie-ben has been delivering important work for Power support for snapshot/restore which is currently going straight into the master branch. Because he doesn't have access to some of the machines/platforms (AIX) he doesn't have a great way of debugging problems other than committers continuously launching PR builds on his behalf.
To cut down on the churn I propose we add him to the whitelist to be able to trigger these builds from GitHub comments.

issue_title: 2m supported large page size on Mac, but not listed in -verbose:sizes
description:
I'm trying to fix the `xlpTests` test on Mac, to run properly and pass. ATM it prints the following, doesn't test any large pages, and passes.
[] Runner couldn't determine underlying OS. Got OS Name:mac os x
[] WARNING: Failed to determine underlying OS. This test needs to know underlying OS.
After adding Mac into the list of platforms, I've run into a snag. The OMR port library for Mac hard codes 3 page sizes into the supported page size table.
1) 4k
2) 0 (zero) with flags OMRPORT_VMEM_PAGE_FLAG_SUPERPAGE_ANY
3) #if defined(VM_FLAGS_SUPERPAGE_SIZE_2MB) - which it is - 2m
The problem is that the `-verbose:sizes` implementation stops when it finds the 0 entry and doesn't include the `2m` entry in the output. However, when the user specifies a large page size, it's validated via vmem_find_valid_page_size() which iterates using the flags field and finds 2m to be a valid size.

issue_title: Consider changing the default javasharedresources directory directly in $HOME
description:
I noticed that since 0.16 the shared cache is on by default (great!) but also that the default directory for the cache has been changed from /tmp/javasharedresources to $HOME/javasharedresources, for understandable reasons.
I and possibly many other Linux desktop users using OpenJ9 don't expect to find this directory directly in their home folder and I would ask to consider moving this directory to one of these locations:
 $HOME/.cache/javasharedresources
 $HOME/.local/share/javasharedresources
This way, the usage of this feature (now on by default) does not clutter up the users' home directory.

issue_title: ValueTypes: Add jit runtime helper to resolve field refs for flatteneable fields
description:
The current jithelpers for flattenable fields require that the fieldrefs for those fields are already resolved. This makes it difficult for the JIT to compile unresolved paths, see To solve this we need to introduce a runtime JIT helper that can be compiled in to unresolved paths which will resolve the flattenable field refs.
This helper will first check if the fieldref is resolved, if not it will attempt to resolve it. Initially this can be implemented using the SLOW_PATH_ONLY_HELPER_NO_RETURN_VALUE template.
Params:
J9VMThread currentThread: implicit param
J9Method method: method in which the resolution must take place
U_32 cpIndex: ram constant pool index for the field ref
U_32 resolveType: one of J9TR_FLAT_RESOLVE_WITHFIELD / J9TR_FLAT_RESOLVE_GETFIELD / J9TR_FLAT_RESOLVE_PUTFIELD
For U_32 parameters on 64-bit platforms, the high-order 32 bits are unused.
jitResolveFlattenableField(...)
To start we should first add the stubs to unblock the JIT progress (see and for an example). In the second phase the actual implementation can be added.

issue_title: DDR overrides don't match VM
description:
On a number of platforms, BOOLEAN is defined as 32-bits.
The following fields are overridden as UDATA, which is not a match on those platforms.
On Windows jdk16, cmdLineTester_modularityddrtests is failing. However it should be failing on all platforms. The test expects java.base packages to be exported to ALL-UNNAMED, but this test is currently invalid for jdk16+ due to JEP 396 "Strongly Encapsulate JDK Internals by Default" changing the defaults. It's not failing on other platforms due to reading a UDATA value as the BOOLEAN, which overlaps the next field in the structure and reads a non-zero value.
From xlinux:
J9Package at <hex> {
 Fields for J9Package:
 <hex>: struct J9UTF8* packageName = !j9utf8 <hex>
 <hex>: UDATA exportToAll = <hex> (0)
 <hex>: UDATA exportToAllUnnamed = <hex> (3749677663984287744)
 <hex>: struct J9Module* module = !j9module <hex>
 <hex>: struct J9HashTable* exportsHashTable = !j9hashtable <hex>
 <hex>: struct J9ClassLoader* classLoader = !j9classloader <hex>
}
Note the field offsets, which show 4 bytes for exportToAll and exportToAllUnnamed. The value of exportToAllUnnamed includes the lower 4 bytes of the next field.
I'm thinking to resolve this particular problem by declaring the fields as U_32 instead of BOOLEAN, and removing the DDR overrides. Also fixing the test for jdk16.

issue_title: DDR should use pointer classes generated at runtime
description:
DDR uses pre-compiled pointer classes generated at build time when using a 64-bit VM to look at a 64-bit core, or 32-bit VM to look at a 32-bit core. It uses pointer classes generated at runtime when there is a mismatch (e.g. 64-bit looking at 32-bit).
The runtime solution can be used always, instead of using the classes generated at build time. We were waiting for all the remaining DDR tests to be ported to open source, and this action has been completed.
