issue_title: JITServer and client should not require write permissions for SSL certificate and key files
description: When JITServer uses encrypted communication, the server and the client read the SSL certificate and keys from files that they open with write permissions. These files are only read by the JITServer and the JVM, and requiring write permissions for them is not something a user would expect.
creator: AlexeyKhrabrov
text:
Bug Title: JITServer and client should not require write permissions for SSL certificate and key files
Bug Description: When JITServer uses encrypted communication, the server and the client read the SSL certificate and keys from files that they open with write permissions. These files are only read by the JITServer and the JVM, and requiring write permissions for them is not something a user would expect.

issue_title: JDK16 : ClassDataTest.java : Incorrect Lookup Access Modes for Hidden Classes
description:
Dependencies to reproduce the error
#11815 and #11816 need to be merged before this error is seen.
 Test source code: ClassDataTest.illegalAccess
 First failure
test ClassDataTest.illegalAccess(java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles$Lookup@2f61e1c0, 31): failure
java.lang.AssertionError: expected [31] but found [15]
 at org.testng.Assert.fail(Assert.java:94)
 at org.testng.Assert.failNotEquals(Assert.java:496)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:125)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:372)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:382)
 at ClassDataTest.illegalAccess(ClassDataTest.java:97)
 Second failure
test ClassDataTest.illegalAccess(java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles$Lookup@c48b6873, 25): failure
java.lang.AssertionError: expected [25] but found [9]
 at org.testng.Assert.fail(Assert.java:94)
 at org.testng.Assert.failNotEquals(Assert.java:496)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:125)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:372)
 at org.testng.Assert.assertEquals(Assert.java:382)
 at ClassDataTest.illegalAccess(ClassDataTest.java:97)
 Notes
1. `MethodHandles.privateLookupIn` and `Lookup.in` incorrectly set access modes for hidden classes. For `privateLookupIn`, `targetClassModule` and `accessClassModule` should be the same. But, they are different in case of OpenJ9. The issue with `Lookup.in` still needs to be investigated.
2. The reported errors are fixed when OJDK MHs are enabled in OpenJ9. So, these failures do not need to be fixed for the JDK16 0.25 release.
3. Re-enable `ClassDataTest.java` after enabling OJDK MHs in OpenJ9. So, should be removed to re-enable `ClassDataTest.java`.

issue_title: Performance evaluation of jdk16+ Class.newInstance()
description:
changes the implementation of Class.newInstance() for jdk16+, which may affect performance. For non-bootstrap callers, instead of calling the newInstanceImpl native, it basically gets the Constructor and calls Constructor.newInstance() instead. There is overhead in getting the reflection object via the reflection cache, and using the reflection optimizations that create new classes.
In all cases, there is the addition of getting the calling class in Class.newInstance().
creator: pshipton
text:
Bug Title: Performance evaluation of jdk16+ Class.newInstance()
Bug Description: changes the implementation of Class.newInstance() for jdk16+, which may affect performance. For non-bootstrap callers, instead of calling the newInstanceImpl native, it basically gets the Constructor and calls Constructor.newInstance() instead. There is overhead in getting the reflection object via the reflection cache, and using the reflection optimizations that create new classes.
In all cases, there is the addition of getting the calling class in Class.newInstance().

issue_title: Enable valhalla as default in VT build
description:
Currently the `-XX:+EnableValhalla` option needs to be turned on to enable value types in the VT build. Given that there has been more progress the JIT and the interpreter this can be enabled by default.
We can keep the option so it can be used for debugging purposes but we can make `-XX:+EnableValhalla` true by default so it doesn't need to be added in test cases.
We will need to update the option parsing code in jvminit.c to make it default. Also we will need to update the test code in `/openj9/test/functional/Valhalla/playlist.xml` to remove the option.
creator: tajila

issue_title: Investigate use of public AzDo in combo with Azure VM agents Jenkins plugin
description:
We believe that we may be able to combine a [public Azure Devops]( for this open-source project (with [unlimited machine minutes]( and up to 10 parallel jobs) with a few Azure Jenkins plugins to create dynamically created test agents to expand the number of xlinux/windows/mac test machines. This issue will track the investigation and work that is required to enable this (if it is indeed possible).
- [ ] Create public AzDo organization
- [ ] Add committers as admins
- [ ] Create a PR to add several Azure plugins to Eclipse Jenkins (similar to but adding azure-commons azure-credentials and azure-vm-agents)
- [ ] Configure public AzDo as a cloud provider to Eclipse Jenkins as per [azure-vm-agents doc]( (EF infra assistance? can raise bugzilla once we know what is required)
- [ ] Change [Jenkinsfilebase]( (currently in Sophia's branch) to call azure-vm-agents when no static machines are idle
- [ ] Verify on xlinux resources first (follow later with others)
- [ ] If we get to this point, review with committers & present in OpenJ9 community call

issue_title: Add jit compile time helper to detect @stable annotation
creator: tajila
text:
Bug Title: Add jit compile time helper to detect @stable annotation
Bug Description: The @stable (java/lang/invoke/Stable) annotation is used an indicator to the JIT that the first non-NULL value stored may be treated as a constant thus enabling constant folding. It behaves similar to final. One difference is that it can also be applied to arrays, meaning that all array elements may be constant folded as well. Currently the only usage of this annotation is in trusted (core JDK) code. Detailed specification can be found in [1].
We will introduced a compile time jithelper to so the JIT can query if the field is annotated with @stable or not.
First we will add a VMHelper
//@param clazz, the class that own the field
//@param the cpindex of the field to query
//@return true, if stable, false otherwise
BOOLEAN
isFieldStable(J9Class clazz, UDATA cpIndex);
Take a look at `dumpAnnotationInfo` in rcdump.c to see how to look up field annotations.
To find the name of the field given a cpIndex `romFieldRef = (J9ROMFieldRef *)&clazz->ramConstantPool->romConstantPool[cpIndex];`
Compile time helpers are stored in cthelpers.cpp
Note: if the static type of the field is an array, then that means all the array elements are considered to be stable. The VM will not do anything special for this. The JIT can recognize this by looking at the static type info.

issue_title: Valhalla: Value type abstract super classes
description:
There is an interface called IndentityObject (currently named `IdentityInterface` - needs renaming) which is implicitly implemented by all stateful types, that is:
1) Is concrete (non-abstract/interface - j.l.Object exculded) or,
2) Declares an instance field or,
3) Declares an instance initializer or,
4) Has constructor with a non-empty body (something other than 'super();') or,
5) Must have access to extend the super class (supers <init> must be visible)
6) Declares a synchronized method
//Note: Most importantly, an abstract class can also implement IdentityInterface explicitly or implicitly if it has any of the properties above
A value-type (primitive class) has the following requirements:
1) Cannot subclass any type that implements `IdentityInterface` either directly or indirectly.
2) Cannot be abstract
3) Must not declare synchronized methods
4) Must have access to extend the super class (supers <init> must be visible)
Currently, we only inject the IdentityObject interface for types that are concrete, This needs to be updated with the new requirements above.
Implementation plan:
1) Detect abstract classes that have no fields, have empty constructors and do not implement `IdentityInterface` either directly or indirectly. We can refer to these as "light" abstract classes, all other abstract classes are considered "heavy"
2) Ensure that all "heavy" abstract classes implement `IdentityInterface`, may inject it if needed. Note "light" abstract classes may optionally implement `IdentityInterface` if user chooses so.
3) Ensure the the super type for Valuetypes is type that doesnt implement `IdentityInterface`, throw a VerificationError otherwise (the exact type of error is TBD but we can use the verify error for the time being)
Test plan
1) Ensure that primitive class can not subclass concrete type or "heavy" abstract type
2) Ensure that primitive class can subclass "light" abstract type and j.l.Object
3) Ensure that primitive class can not subtype IndentityObject
4) Ensure that primitive class can not subclass any type that implements IdentityObject (even if light abstract type) either directly or indirectly
5) Ensure primitive class can not be abstract or interface
6) Ensure primitive class can not have synchronized methods
//Note: some of the existing tests in `openj9/test/functional/Valhalla/src/org/openj9/test/lworld/ValueTypeTests.java` may need to be modified with the new requirements.

issue_title: Jenkins job to delete obsolete jenkins jobs
description: To keep a handle on the number of jenkins jobs, and reduce disk space usage on master (i.e. we need to create a jenkins job that can delete obsolete jenkins jobs based on a pattern. There are hundreds of jobs per version, and we also introduce special jobs for OMH, mixed, cm, uma, xl, etc, which become obsolete. Trying to delete all the jobs manually is very painful. The delete job needs to take a pattern to control what is deleted so we can customize it as needed. It would be useful to have two modes, 1) list all the jobs that match the pattern, for confirmation the pattern will delete the correct things 2) delete them.

issue_title: Track Progress of Low-pause GC - Concurrent Copy Forward
description:
Track Progress of Low-pause GC Concurrent Copy Forward
The purpose of this issue is to keep track of development of low-pause Garbage Collector (GC) - concurrent copy forward, and conduct any discussions as necessary. The following is a rough plan of what’s to come. This plan is subject to modifications as new findings/development progress. - [ ] Refactor/organize `IncrementalGenerationalGG` / `CopyForward` code - [ ] Introduce `MM_ConcurrentCopyForwardSchemeTask` which is the equivalent of Concurrent Scavenger `MM_ConcurrentScavengeTask`. Also introduce CopyForward state machine that will dictate concurrent CopyForward phase transitions. - [ ] First phase of Concurrent Partial GC (PGC): divide current PGC into 3 separate Stop the World (STW) phases and start to make use of introduced concurrent CopyForward code from above. These 3 STW phases (`STW -> STW -> STW`) will eventually become 2 STW phases and one middle concurrent phase (`STW -> concurrent -> STW`)
- [ ] Introduce read barriers
- [ ] Second phase of Concurrent PGC: start to make use of read barriers to transition to `STW -> concurrent -> STW` phase
- [ ] Switch Global Marking Phase (GMP) to use Snapshot-At-The-Beginning (SATB) style Write barrier
Additional details/plan for Concurrent Copy Forward goal:
- PGC what is an evacuating style of GC will be made concurrent. Load Reference Barrier will be triggered on region check via a look up table. As it's the case already (with STW variant), it will be by default an one-pass GC, where references outside of Collection Set are fixed during the Remembered Set (RS) scan phase.
- GMP will be converted to use SATB style Write barrier to avoid final STW Card Clearing phase
- Sweep (as an explicit STW operation piggybacked to first PGC after GMP is completed) will be eliminated.

issue_title: Document usage of J9VMThread.tempSlot field
description:
`vmThread->tempSlot` is used in multiple places and for different purposes. More uses of this field has been introduced recently in #10617 and #12034, for example. However, there is currently no unified documentation listing the use of this overloaded field, increasing the risk of introducing changes that cause an overwrite that results unexpected outcomes. The purpose of this issue is to track the work around documenting the uses of this field, similar to how the overloaded J9Method.extra field is documented in #12045. According to a [review comment]( in #12034, the documentation should answer the following:
1. What are all the uses of this field?
2. How can I be sure that the value I store here will not be overwritten by some other piece of code which wants to use this same field?

issue_title: Enable native code coverage for openj9
description: Code coverage provides very important piece of information about where to focus our testing. It will help to identify testing gaps which will help to reduce escaped defects, reduce the number of PMRs, and user-raised issues. We can also use this native code coverage to do changed-based testing in the future. This is especially useful during new feature development.

issue_title: JVM sometimes hangs when calling kill -QUIT <javapid>
description:
Java -version output
Output from `java -version`.
# java --version
openjdk 11.0.10 2021-01-19
OpenJDK Runtime Environment AdoptOpenJDK (build 11.0.10+9)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM AdoptOpenJDK (build openj9-0.24.0, JRE 11 Linux amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20210120_910 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 345e1b09e
OMR - 741e94ea8
JCL - 0a86953833 based on jdk-11.0.10+9)
Summary of problem
We have a tomcat instance that randomly hangs. We narrowed this down to when our docker health check is failing, which in turn does a `pkill -3 java` so that we could diagnose _why_ our health checks were getting stuck. However, it appears that sometimes when doing this the JVM just freezes, and nothing happens anymore. `jstack` gives no results.
We can force this to occur with the following:
$ while true; do pkill -3 java; done
Typically this does within a few hundred thread dumps, although I have had it once generate almost 3000. I have never had this not fail within about 10 minutes.
Diagnostic files
There is no crash, nor is there any output.
Given that we _can_ reproduce this 100%, we can test and/or retrieve information that might help to diagnose the issue.

issue_title: sanity.system ExplMod fails due to unexpected java.lang.IllegalAccessError message text
description:
openj9's `java.lang.IllegalAccessError` message text differs from hotpot's, and that causes the ExplMod system test (currently excluded) to fail.
The test was presumably calibrated against hotspot, and while the text which accompanies an exception is up to the implementor to specify I assume openj9 would like to consider whether to make changes to its message before requesting that the test case be changed.
This is the openj9 exception message thrown when running the test:
java.lang.IllegalAccessError: Class net/adoptopenjdk/test/modularity/junit/TestImpliedReadability(module com.test) can not access class org/hamcrest/CoreMatchers(module hamcrest.core) because module module com.test does not read module module hamcrest.core
It is the duplication of the word `module` (as in `module module hamcrest.core`) which causes the test to fail,
I notice the openj9 message also includes slashes rather than dots in the referenced class name.
See for more details.

issue_title: Add a new option for jextract so that it does not bundle the system core file.
description:
Very often in Service, we have received system core files from customers without the native libraries, and we have to go back to customer asking them to do jextract again. The jextracted files can be huge (and often a few GB) and it is not easy for customer to upload the huge file. If jextract provides a special option (such as "-excludeCore") to exclude the system core file from the jextract result, then the jextract file normally only a few MB. This would make it much easier for customers to upload the jextract result.
If the system core file is excluded from the jextract result, it would be better if we can add a text file which documents the system core file filename, target system info (something similar to the output from jdmpview command "info sys"). This will avoid confusions.
Of course, this new option should be off by default. And this option is to be used only after we have had the un-jextracted system core file from customer. Unfortunately this scenario is very common in service world.

issue_title: Improve DDR compatibility story for fields
description:
There was some discussion in about improving the DDR compatibility story for fields, somewhat similar to the work done for constants via One idea is to limit generation of methods for new fields at build time, requiring them to be added to a compatibility file. The compatibility file contains instructions to developers that use of fields added to the file need to handle NoSuchFieldError / NoSuchMethodError since the field doesn't exist in older core files. Adding to the compatibility file is also a reminder to reviewers to ensure that new fields are handled properly for compatibility.
Another idea is for the code generated for newer fields to throw a checked Exception that needs to be handled by callers. This ensures that callers added either when the field is added or later need to think about it and handle the exception. Reviewers would see the exception handling and know to check the fields are handled properly for compatibility.

issue_title: Javacores need timezone information for the 1TIDATETIME field
description:
The `1TIDATETIME` field in javacores currently looks like this:
1TIDATETIME Date: 2021/04/09 at :106
This information is presented in the local timezone at the OS level, which is absolutely fine, but we have no way of knowing what that timezone is, unless it has been set explicitly in an environment variable such as `TZ`. When troubleshooting, this can make it tricky to correlate javacores with other data, which may have timestamps presented in different timezones.
So it would be very useful if the `1TIDATETIME` field included the timezone, or perhaps a new field specifically for the timezone would be more appropriate (to avoid breaking anyone who parses the `1TIDATETIME` field).

issue_title: Descriptions of release semantics are wrong in javadoc for VarHandle methods
description:
`releaseFence` ensures that loads/stores before the fence will not be reordered with stores after the fence, but javadoc states differently.
Similarly, `setRelease` sets the value using `release` semantics, which ensures that preceding loads/stores will not be reordered after the store, but javadoc states differently.
creator: Akira1Saitoh
text:
Bug Title: Descriptions of release semantics are wrong in javadoc for VarHandle methods
Bug Description: `releaseFence` ensures that loads/stores before the fence will not be reordered with stores after the fence, but javadoc states differently.
Similarly, `setRelease` sets the value using `release` semantics, which ensures that preceding loads/stores will not be reordered after the store, but javadoc states differently.

issue_title: Explore doing a GC compaction before taking snapshot
description: Doing a GC compaction may be one way of reducing the size of the snapshot that gets generated. This expectation needs to be validated first and then depending on the results we may need to consider doing a compaction and/or any other GC optimization we feel would be appropriate to either reduce the size of the snapshot or to improve the performance after restore. Another possible pre-snapshot option might be to zero out memory if this encourages a better compression ratio when we take the snapshot. This direction also needs to be explored first before to check what kind of compression (if any) happens at snapshot creation time.

issue_title: java/util/Random default constructor behaviour in snapshot mode
description:
Restoring from a given snapshot that has a java/util/Random seeded with the same value will result in the same sequence of random numbers generated when using the `nextInt` API as one example (there are others). This is guaranteed by the API doc at : This makes the behaviour of java/util/Random tricky for the default constructor API that says:
`Creates a new random number generator. This constructor sets the seed of the random number generator to a value very likely to be distinct from any other invocation of this constructor.`
This can cause issues from an end user perspective in that a seed chosen during the snapshot run is reused in every run based on a restore from a given snapshot. Note that the non-default constructor that passes in a seed expects the same sequence of random numbers to be generated from this class. So we need to examine what can be done to preserve the necessary determinism for the non-default constructor case while still preserving the desired random-ness for the default constructor case when running in snapshot mode.

description:

`NoSuchMethodError` thrown from `MethodHandleResolver.getCPMethodHandleAt`.
test TestNative.testNativeAccess(TestNative$$Lambda$108/<hex>@9414ac56, TestNative$$Lambda$101/<hex>@15d3e380, [100:b8]): failure
java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: java/lang/invoke/VarHandle.get(Ljdk/incubator/foreign/MemorySegment;Ljava/lang/Long;)Ljava/lang/Object; (loaded from jrt:/java.base by <Bootstrap Loader>) called from class TestNative (loaded from file:/.../openjdk-tests/TKG/output_16171331559140/jdk_custom_0/work/classes/0/java/foreign/TestNative.d/ by jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@3144ebb).
 at java.base/java.lang.invoke.MethodHandleResolver.getCPMethodHandleAt(Native Method)
 at java.base/java.lang.invoke.MethodHandleResolver.getAdditionalBsmArg(MethodHandleResolver.java:382)
 at java.base/java.lang.invoke.MethodHandleResolver.resolveInvokeDynamic(MethodHandleResolver.java:181)
 at TestNative.lambda$nativeAccessOps$17(TestNative.java:243)
 at TestNative$$Lambda$108/<hex>.accept(Unknown Source)
 at TestNative.testNativeAccess(TestNative.java:159)
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.NativeMethodAccessorImpl.invoke0(Native Method)
 Initial Investigation
`VarHandle.get` is a `VarHandle MH/VH polymorphic method`. The above stack suggests that `invokedynamic` is invoked on `VarHandle.get`, which should never happen. For MH/VH `polymorphic` methods, the correct bytecode is `invokevirtual` which gets rewritten to `invokehandle`. Here, a `Lambda` is also involved. For `Lambdas`, OJDK code dynamically generates the bytecodes. Below, `invokedynamic` on `VarHandle.get` is called from `Lambda generated bytecodes`. We will need to investigate why `Lambda` generated bytecodes are calling `invokedynamic` on `VarHandle.get`.
`Lambda bytecode generation`: Run Failing Test: TestNative.java

make test TEST="java/foreign/TestNative.java"

issue_title: Preserve entire contents of XMM registers across helper calls on X
description:
To support vectorization, the entire 16-byte contents of each XMM register must be preserved in the JIT helpers (currently only 64 bits of FPR parameter registers are preserved).
The helpers will be divided as they were on P into method call and non-method call points. At method call points, only 8 bytes of the parameter XMMs will be preserved so the decompiler can see the contents properly. All non-paramteter XMMs will have all 16 bytes preserved.
There is no need to check the vector flag on X as all supported processors support the full-width XMM registers.
creator: gacholio
text:
Bug Title: Preserve entire contents of XMM registers across helper calls on X
Bug Description: To support vectorization, the entire 16-byte contents of each XMM register must be preserved in the JIT helpers (currently only 64 bits of FPR parameter registers are preserved).
The helpers will be divided as they were on P into method call and non-method call points. At method call points, only 8 bytes of the parameter XMMs will be preserved so the decompiler can see the contents properly. All non-paramteter XMMs will have all 16 bytes preserved.
There is no need to check the vector flag on X as all supported processors support the full-width XMM registers.

issue_title: [OJDK MH] Investigate if @FrameIteratorSkip bit can be claimed for perf
description:
Ref: > RI tags methods with `@PolymorphicSignature` annotation during ClassFile parsing. So, they only have to do a bit test for identifying polymorphic methods in native code. On the other hand, OJ9 has to compare class and method names for identifying polymorphic methods since it does not have extra bits to tag methods. The above `MethodHandleNatives.init` string comparisons will be repeated from `MemberName`'s constructor: OJ9 will do the `strcmps` twice, which can be improved in the future.
Ref: > The `@FrameIteratorSkip` is only used by the OJ9 implementation of MH. Can we reclaim the `@FrameIteratorSkip` annotation and its associated bit for use by `@PolymorphicSignature` methods? This will lead to better performance.

issue_title: [OJDK MH] AccessControl Issues from ClassDefiner.defineClass
description:
Description
Improper handling of `AccessControl` privileges from `MethodHandles$Lookup$ClassDefiner.defineClass` leads to either an `AccessControlException` (Error 1) or `StackOverflowError` (Error 2) depending on the test case. There is no micro-test or open-sourced test case to reproduce this failure. So, this issue has been opened to track internal failures.

> **OJDK MHs** uses `ClassDefiner` to define normal and hidden classes whereas **OJ9 MHs** uses `ClassDefiner` only to define hidden classes: In OJDK MHs, the above hack also impacts the `ClassDefiner.defineClass` code path for defining normal (non-hidden) classes. `SecurityExceptions` do not get thrown for normal classes due to the `AccessController.doPrivileged` from `ClassDefiner.defineClass`.

issue_title: Mixedrefs build not switching to nocompressedrefs automatically based on -Xmx
description:
Use any latest build, or the 0.26 release.
`java -Xmx300g` gives an error `VMJ9GC028E Option too large: '-Xmx'`
`java -Xnocompressedrefs -Xmx300g` works fine.
Since there is only one JVM in the package, I don't think it's a problem with the redirector. It seems the VM is missing logic outside the redirector to check the -Xmx value and NOT set the J9_EXTENDED_RUNTIME2_COMPRESS_OBJECT_REFERENCES flag.
@dmitripivkine @tajila fyi

issue_title: Shared class cache name and number of connected users not available through APIs
description:
Requirement for the current JVM's resolved shared class cache name and number of connected users to be added to the MemoryMXBean and SharedClass APIs (com.ibm.oti.shared.SharedClassStatistics and com.ibm.oti.shared.SharedClassUtilities) so this information can be recorded in CICS JVM server statistics reports.
The resolved shared class cache name is not available today in the openJ9 SharedClass APIs or the MemoryMXBean. Only the unresolved shared class cache name is obtainable through the Java system API, via the -Xshareclasses:name=<> JVM option. The resolved cache name is valuable as CICS is unable to resolve the symbols that can be specified in the cache name. The number of users connected to the SCC is already available from the openJ9 java core, but it is not available from the SharedClass APIs. This limits CICS from capturing this information and reporting it in its statistics report. This information is valuable as it allows customers to confirm if the class cache is being shared by other JVMs, which would prevent the cache from being deleted until the connected JVMs are stopped.

issue_title: Replace x86/libffi in OpenJ9 to the latest version
description:
The code of `x86/libffi` in OpenJ9 remains unchanged since 2013 and becomes obsolete given the latest updated code occurs earlier this year at (most of code were rewritten & the code on Windows was totally replaced with the newer version). Even though the older version satisfies the needs of the existing code in OpenJ9 but it fails to correctly support the struct/nested struct with special handling in padding/alignment, which is required by the work on JEP389 at The initial investigation on `Linux/x86_64` with looks very promising because it resolves the majority of the alignment issues detected with our test cases on Linux.
Given there should be no impact on the existing code in terms of standard interface/public APIs exploited in OpenJ9, I propose to replace the older version in OpenJ9 with the latest one (the master branch by default). There is no 100% guarantee that the replacement fixes all issues detected in our tests but it is worth to do so to address as many struct-related issues as we can in this way. Thus, this issue is created to keep track of the replacement work and any issue/PR related to the work. In addition, we might need to evaluate the results for the existing code with the newer version (In theory it shouldn't but we should keep any eye on this in case anything unexpected occurs after the replacement)
The code is specific to Linux/x86_64 and Windows/x86_64.
FYI: @mstoodle, @tajila, @pshipton, @gacholio, @DanHeidinga, @dnakamura

issue_title: JVM restore hook needs to ensure that we obey environment variables
description:
Linux (and probably most other OSes) processes pick up the environment variable values as specified at the time the process was started. In other words, if some environment variable changes in value after the process starts up, this is not visible to the process since its view of the environment variables is what was initialized at process start time.
This behavior also translates to processes that get restored by CRIU not picking up environment variables from the restored environment, and instead using environment variables as specified in the snapshot environment. This can be a problem in the restore environment that may wish to specify a different locale or some other property relevant to the application via environment variables.
This problem is really to be viewed as two separate cases probably :
1) Java code that wants to read environment variables which typically goes through System or ProcessEnvironment classes/apis for doing so.
2) OpenJ9 code that wants to read environment variables which typically calls native api via the port library interface, e.g. something that controls options in use or something that controls whether a particular JIT transformation will be done or not. OpenJ9 needs to handle both cases by scraping the environment variables from the restore environment (crudely speaking by doing an exec call to `printenv` and then parsing the key/value mappings from the output and using the result rather than relying on the OS returning the values in the restore environment OR some other better technique to achieve the same end result) so that the restored JVM adapts as expected from an end-user perspective. Specifically, this means hiding this issue from Java code (such as Open Liberty) that should transparently be given the values from the restore environment.

issue_title: Re-enable excluded vtstandard tests
description:
Use this issue to track tests temporarily excluded in `x86-64_linux_vt_standard` build. See Currently `AnnotationInvocationHandler` enforces annotation type to have `java.lang.annotation.Annotation.class` as its only super interface. This is not true anymore after #12039.
`org.openj9.test.annotationPackage.Test_PackageAnnotation` and `org.openj9.test.annotationPackage.Test_PackageAnnotation2` are excluded in x86-64_linux_vt_standard build for now. They can be re-enabled after `AnnotationInvocationHandler` is changed in JCL for value type.

issue_title: NoClassDefFoundError: openj9.dtfj module conflicts with uses of ibmjzos.jar on platforms other than z/OS
description:
Hi OpenJ9 team,
on z/OS, the JZOS classes are part of the **ibm.jzos** Java module, just as expected. On platforms other than z/OS, OpenJ9 only contains a stub of the `com.ibm.jzos.ZFile` class, which is part of the **openj9.dtfj** Java module. This leads to problems when JZOS is being used on platforms other than z/OS.
Please note that this is **not** a hypothetical use case - there is at least one customer that I am aware of who actually makes use of some JZOS classes on a non-z/OS operating system.
On OpenJ9 versions up to and including **0.24.0**, the following test works as expected:
marc@localhost:~$ jdk-11.0.10+9/bin/java -cp /path/to/ibmjzos.jar com.ibm.jzos.FileFactory
Error: Main method not found in class com.ibm.jzos.FileFactory, please define the main method as:
 public static void main(String[] args)
or a JavaFX application class must extend javafx.application.Application
Whereas on OpenJ9 versions **> 0.24.0**, the same test leads to an error:
marc@localhost:~$ jdk-11.0.11+9/bin/java -cp /path/to/ibmjzos.jar com.ibm.jzos.FileFactory
Error: Could not find or load main class com.ibm.jzos.FileFactory
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.ibm.jzos.FileFactory
The root cause of this problem seems to be the inclusion of the `com.ibm.jzos.ZFile` class into the **openj9.dtfj** Java module, which dictates the visibility of the `com.ibm.jzos` package.
Is there a way to restore the old behavior?
Cheers,
Marc

issue_title: jextract libraries with newer releases
description:
In recent releases the java executable on Linux platforms was changed from an executable to a shared library. This results in changes to the information held in system corefiles relating to libraries that were in use by the process at the time of the crash. Tools such as jextract and others were modified to compensate for these changes, but we're noticing some problems in the resulting output.
a) Missing libraries - not all libraries seem to be collected reliably. In particular the jit library is often missing in the jextract zipfile. Other, non-JVM libraries may also be missing.
b) Libraries that were loaded via symbolic links appear in the zipfile with the name and location of the link. This present a challenge for tools that consume the data as the library name and path that appears in the NT_FILE data of the system corefile is that of the actual library, not the symlink.
Both of these problems can be worked around for most cases, but it would be great if it's possible to stream-line this for future releases.

issue_title: Atomic flag for valuetypes
description:
ACC_ATOMIC class modifier
In a class file with version number 61.65535, the ACC_ATOMIC flag may be applied to a primitive class to require that instances be handled atomically when inlined in a variable or array. In a class file with any other version number, the <hex> bit is ignored, and the ACC_ATOMIC flag is considered not to be set. If the ACC_ATOMIC flag is set, the ACC_PRIMITIVE flag must also be set.
This may eventually be changed to an Interface, but the JVM behaviour will still be the same

issue_title: Update jitGetClassInClassloaderFromUTF8 to find hidden classes
description:
The JIT currently uses `jitGetClassInClassloaderFromUTF8` to look up classes based on signatures. It is need to get the type of method args. This API uses `hashClassTableAt` to lookup classes, however, if it is looking up a hidden class it returns NULL. We need to provide a way for the JIT to find hidden classes.
Given how often `hashClassTableAt` is used we may want to create a new version `hashClassTableAtImpl` that has no HIDDEN_CLASS checks which can be called by the `hashClassTableAt` version.

issue_title: Make sure the right file descriptor information is persisted for restore in containers
description:
We need to handle this scenario that Younes investigated and summarized:
The problem I was seeing with stdout/stderr boils down to: when you start a container in detached mode docker will pipe your process' output to some file(s). Your process stdout/stderr will be attached to two anonymous pipes at dump time. At restore, since we're starting a new container, the restored process will be piped to new file and its stdout/stderr will be pointing at two new anonymous pipes. The problem is that criu doesn't know that the old pipes and new pipes are the same logical outputs and things can go wrong if we try to access them. At dump time we have to remember which of our file descriptors are attached to pipes and at restore time we have to tell criu which current file descriptors map to the remembered pipes using the --inherit-fd fd[x]:pipe:[y] option. Once I do that I can save and restore the process and the output is where it's supposed to be.
In a discussion this week it was felt that we should be writing out the FD information for stdout/stderr in some format would be handled by OpenJ9 (other piped FDs if there exist any would only be known to the Java application and it would have to handle those explicitly) so that the "caller of CRIU restore" (e.g. some script on the Open Liberty side) issues the CRIU restore command with this information passed in. FYI @tajila and @ymanton
creator: vijaysun-omr

issue_title: Reduce HCR impact on the effectiveness of escape analysis
description:
HCR (Hot Code Replace) is enabled by default in OpenJ9 and makes the escape analysis optimization in the JIT compiler more conservative. The affected part of escape analysis is primarily the method peeking logic, that is essentially disabled at levels below the top level call. This is related to two things
1) Peeking of methods is fundamentally limited in a run where HCR is enabled because the result of peeking cannot be used by the analysis without some means of compensating for the case when the peeked method gets changed due to a class/method redefinition in the future
2) The ability to compensate for peeked methods changing is limited to the top level call Ii.e. a call that is in the IL trees when escape analysis is run) since that is the only call for which we are generating code in the compiled method. The IL for peeked methods at lower levels of the call graph are only examined during the course of the method peeking and are discarded after the method peek is over (thereby also losing any ability to compensate for any changes at those lower levels due to redefinition). At the top level call, a change was made last year that essentially guards a peeked method with an HCR guard and if we redefined the method being called, then the guard would be patched to take a slow path that performs a heapification before calling the redefined method (following a similar scheme to what we do for guarded inlined calls (on a cold path) and cold block heapification in escape analysis already).
Given this inability to peek methods at lower levels of the call graph when HCR is enabled, escape analysis is still not at anywhere close to full effectiveness by default (since HCR is enabled by default). This issue aims to address this and offer a way for escape analysis to become as effective as before HCR was enabled by default in the expected common case when no classes are actually being redefined by the user. The proposal is to allow escape analysis to peek methods at levels lower in the call graph, and define a scheme whereby we track which compiled methods have had objects stack allocated based on method peeked at lower levels of the call graph.
In the unlikely event that any class gets redefined (we can optionally also track the list of classes that are relevant to escape analysis' peeking if we wanted to be more accurate), the VM would need to do a few things at the class redefinition event (before "activating" the redefined class)
1. Invalidate all the compiled bodies that relied on peeking to stack allocate objects 2. OSR out of all such compiled bodies and transition to the interpreter
3. Heapify all stack allocated objects dynamically by allocating new heap objects and copying over the contents from the corresponding stack allocated objects. Update all registers and stack slots that pointed at a stack allocated object to instead point at the corresponding heap allocated object.
This kind of a scheme would allow escape analysis to become more aggressive in the presence of HCR and still maintain functional correctness. @tajila and @<hex>ryl fyi

In the unlikely event that any class gets redefined (we can optionally also track the list of classes that are relevant to escape analysis' peeking if we wanted to be more accurate), the VM would need to do a few things at the class redefinition event (before "activating" the redefined class)
1. Invalidate all the compiled bodies that relied on peeking to stack allocate objects 2. OSR out of all such compiled bodies and transition to the interpreter
3. Heapify all stack allocated objects dynamically by allocating new heap objects and copying over the contents from the corresponding stack allocated objects. Update all registers and stack slots that pointed at a stack allocated object to instead point at the corresponding heap allocated object.
This kind of a scheme would allow escape analysis to become more aggressive in the presence of HCR and still maintain functional correctness. @tajila and @<hex>ryl fyi

issue_title: Reduce HCR impact on the effectiveness of escape analysis
description:
HCR (Hot Code Replace) is enabled by default in OpenJ9 and makes the escape analysis optimization in the JIT compiler more conservative. The affected part of escape analysis is primarily the method peeking logic, that is essentially disabled at levels below the top level call. This is related to two things
1) Peeking of methods is fundamentally limited in a run where HCR is enabled because the result of peeking cannot be used by the analysis without some means of compensating for the case when the peeked method gets changed due to a class/method redefinition in the future
2) The ability to compensate for peeked methods changing is limited to the top level call Ii.e. a call that is in the IL trees when escape analysis is run) since that is the only call for which we are generating code in the compiled method. The IL for peeked methods at lower levels of the call graph are only examined during the course of the method peeking and are discarded after the method peek is over (thereby also losing any ability to compensate for any changes at those lower levels due to redefinition). At the top level call, a change was made last year that essentially guards a peeked method with an HCR guard and if we redefined the method being called, then the guard would be patched to take a slow path that performs a heapification before calling the redefined method (following a similar scheme to what we do for guarded inlined calls (on a cold path) and cold block heapification in escape analysis already).

issue_title: Extend line endings check
description:
Changes in pull requests are checked for proper line endings: LF for most text files or CR/LF for some Windows-specific text files.
I propose that we extend those checks to ensure that each added or modified line has no trailing whitespace or unnecessary blank lines at EOF.
Since the inception of this project I have yet to see a legitimate need for trailing whitespace in any file. On the other hand, trailing whitespace can lead to some difficult to recognize problems.
Consider this sequence in [jvmtiMethod.c](
#define FLIP_32BIT(index) \
 do { \
 bytecodes[(index) + 0] = j9Bytecodes[(index) + 3]; \
 bytecodes[(index) + 1] = j9Bytecodes[(index) + 2]; \
 bytecodes[(index) + 2] = j9Bytecodes[(index) + 1]; \
 bytecodes[(index) + 3] = j9Bytecodes[(index) + 0]; \
 } while(0)
If the first line had trailing whitespace (after the `\`), `gcc` would complain:
jvmtiMethod.c:750:27: error: backslash and newline separated by space [-Werror]
 #define FLIP_32BIT(index) \
On the other hand, if a space was present after the second of these lines in [OpenJ9.gmk](
 +BOOT_JDK=$(BOOT_JDK) $(EXPORT_COMPILER_ENV_VARS) OPENJDK_VERSION_NUMBER_FOUR_POSITIONS=$(VERSION_NUMBER_FOUR_POSITIONS) \
 $(MAKE) $(MAKE_ARGS) -C $(OUTPUTDIR)/vm -f $(OPENJ9_TOPDIR)/runtime/buildtools.mk \
an UMA build would fail:
cc -o .o
cc: fatal error: no input files
compilation terminated.
<builtin>: recipe for target '.o' failed
Not many people will successfully trace that back to the offending space.

issue_title: Cannot build jdk with recent openj9 bootjdk
description:
Using a recent bootjdk (e.g. jdk11-openj9-0.27.0) leads to failure building the current jdk11:
Generating DDR pointer and structure class files
Missing required field: MM_MemoryPoolBumpPointer._allocatePointer
This appears to be caused by the copy of `AuxFieldInfo29.dat` found in the bootjdk instead of the source tree which says
MM_MemoryPoolBumpPointer._allocatePointer = required
instead of
MM_MemoryPoolBumpPointer._allocatePointer = void*

issue_title: Improve performance of StackWalker.walk
description:
## Background Context
Through a customer engagement we've identified a bottleneck in OpenJ9's stack walking implementation. Using the [apache/logging-log4j2]( framework we've built the following simple JMH benchmark which is representative bottleneck in the customer workload:
package org.openj9;
import org.apache.logging.log4j.LogManager;
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.*;
import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
@Fork(value = 1)
@Warmup(iterations = 10, time = 2000, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
@Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 1000, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
public class Log4jGetLoggerBenchmark {
 public static org.apache.logging.log4j.Logger log4jLogger;
 @Benchmark
 public void testGetLoggerBasic() {
 log4jLogger = LogManager.getLogger("JJ.510845011882325196");
 }
}
At a high level the [`LogManager.getLogger`]( API invokes [`java/lang/StackWalker.walk`]( API to apply a [filter]( which I'll inline here:
 public Class<?> getCallerClass(final String fqcn, final String pkg) {
 return walker.walk(s -> s.dropWhile(f -> !f.getClassName().equals(fqcn))
 .dropWhile(f -> f.getClassName().equals(fqcn))
 .dropWhile(f -> !f.getClassName().startsWith(pkg))
 .findFirst())
 .map(StackWalker.StackFrame::getDeclaringClass).orElse(null);
 }
This filter effectively looks for the name of the caller class of the `LogManager.getLogger` API call. In the above JMH benchmark it is looking for the class name `"Log4jGetLoggerBenchmark"`.
## Java 8 vs. Java 11
According to the [documentation]( due to the deprecation of the `getCallerClass(int)` API in Java 8, the log4j library had to roll out an alternative way of extracting the class name of the caller. It rolled out the [`StackLocator`]( implementation which is the source of a Java 8 vs. Java 11 regression.
A quick measurement on Linux x86-64 reproduces the delta:
JDK 1.8.0_302, Eclipse OpenJ9 VM, openj9-0.27.0:
Benchmark Mode Cnt Score Error Units
Log4jGetLoggerBenchmark.testGetLoggerBasic thrpt 3 129065.089 ± 2370.504 ops/s
JDK 11.0.12, Eclipse OpenJ9 VM, openj9-0.27.0:
Benchmark Mode Cnt Score Error Units
Log4jGetLoggerBenchmark.testGetLoggerBasic thrpt 3 90105.024 ± 35967.100 ops/s
## Profiling
Grabbing a `perf record` profile with call-graph information of the Java 11 case shows clearly where the bottleneck is:
Samples: 5K of event 'cycles', Event count (approx.): 1803867237
 Children Self Command Shared Object Symbol
- 67.15% 4.34% org.openj9.Log4 libjclse29.so [.] Java_java_lang_StackWalker_getImpl - Java_java_lang_StackWalker_getImpl - 36.66% j9gc_createJavaLangString - 16.01% MM_StringTable::hashAtUTF8 - MM_StringTable::hashAt - hashTableFind - 14.32% comparatorToEqualFn stringComparatorFn + 3.13% monitor_exit.part.10 + 2.79% monitor_enter_three_tier.constprop.17 + 11.57% J9AllocateObject + 5.17% walkStackFrames + 2.98% getLineNumberForROMClassFromROMMethod 2.62% J9WriteBarrierStore + 1.36% getOriginalROMMethod 1.13% MM_GenerationalAccessBarrierComponent::postObjectStore 0.59% MM_StandardAccessBarrier::postObjectStoreImpl + 36.66% 13.83% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] j9gc_createJavaLangString + 16.01% 0.05% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] MM_StringTable::hashAtUTF8 + 15.97% 0.23% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] MM_StringTable::hashAt + 15.74% 1.21% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] hashTableFind + 14.32% 0.34% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] comparatorToEqualFn + 14.00% 1.78% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] J9AllocateObject + 13.98% 13.96% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] stringComparatorFn + 11.63% 2.57% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] OMR_GC_AllocateObject + 7.96% 0.46% org.openj9.Log4 libj9vm29.so [.] walkStackFrames + 7.71% 0.39% org.openj9.Log4 libjclse29.so [.] Java_java_lang_StackWalker_walkWrapperImpl
+ 7.38% 0.75% org.openj9.Log4 libj9jit29.so [.] jitWalkStackFrames + 5.31% 0.62% org.openj9.Log4 libj9gc29.so [.] MM_TLHAllocationInterface::allocateObject The perf report is telling us pretty much to focus on the children inside the `Java_java_lang_StackWalker_getImpl` function:
More specifically these calls to `utfToStringObject` which end up calling `j9gc_createJavaLangString`. Looking at just that function it has 1/3 of time spent in itself and 2/3 spent in its children (`MM_StringTable::hashAt*` being the biggest offenders).
Looking further into the annotation of `j9gc_createJavaLangString` we can see we are interning all of these strings and getting hits in the hash table as there are no ticks following the call to `hashAtUTF8` until the rest of the method.
This means we are skipping this entire if statement:
All this makes sense.
The bottleneck appears to be from attempting to create the strings representing the method name and signature. Because previous invocations have interned such strings we are doing full string comparisons and matching entries in the interned string hash table. This is why we see lots of ticks coming from `stringComparatorFn`. Additionally we are recomputing the hash values of the UTF8 strings so we can carry out a hash table lookup every time.
## Previous Work
We do cache the class name in the `java/lang/Class` object for fast lookup:
As can be seen here in the `getImpl` stack walker code:
This work was carried out by @DanHeidinga as part of #7776. Unfortunately there isn’t a natural fit for the method and signature strings as there is no backing object in that case.
## Additional Tracing
We took a broad look at the APIs and how things piece together. From our understanding we construct the walk state for the stack walk in `java/lang/StackWalker.walkWrapperImpl` and much deeper down the stack we call `java/lang/StackWalker.getImpl` which actually populates the `StackFrame` object with the class name, method name, and method signature. An important detail is that the walkstate was constructed in frame `[14]` in the above snippet, so the first time we call getImpl the class + method + signature that gets populated is actually frame `[16]`. We don’t fully understand why it is not `[15]` but the data shows it clearly. We placed an NLS trace inside of the native implementation of `Java_java_lang_StackWalker_getImpl` and here is what we see:

JVMDUMP053I org/apache/logging/log4j/LogManager.getContext(Z)Lorg/apache/logging/log4j/spi/LoggerContext;
JVMDUMP053I org/apache/logging/log4j/LogManager.getLogger(Ljava/lang/String;)Lorg/apache/logging/log4j/Logger;
JVMDUMP053I Test.foo()V
This matches that of the method trace output. It appears there is a total of **9 frames** that get traversed before the filter from log4j matches the frame we are looking for. This number is static because the callees never change.
## Potential Solutions
Ideally we'd like to eliminate the cost of calling `j9gc_createJavaLangString` and the various hashing/hash table lookup APIs. This is possible since 9/10 stack frames in this case will always be the same and the strings representing the methods and signatures are interned. A natural solution is to use a cache for these objects.
- Option 1: Introduce a small (~10ish element) thread local least recently used (LRU) cache mapping ROM method pointers to a pair of `java.lang.String` objects representing the method name and signature. This cache would be populated and used in `Java_java_lang_StackWalker_getImpl` for fast retrieval of these values which should eliminate much of the performance cost.
- Option 2: Same as above except using a global cache. This will require some form of locking.
- Option 3: Create a hashmap on the Java side in `java/lang/Class` which is lazily populated with the key being a `long` representing the ROM method pointer, and the value being the pair of method name and signature. This solution allows us to reuse such a cache in other places within the JVM, i.e. `getStackTrace` API.
- Option 4: Rather than using a cache, attempt to recover some of the performance by improving the hashing functions, and the string comparison functions. Perhaps caching the hash of the UTF8 string on the RAM/ROM method could save cycles as well.
- Option 5: Other suggestions?

Ideally we'd like to eliminate the cost of calling `j9gc_createJavaLangString` and the various hashing/hash table lookup APIs. - Option 3: Create a hashmap on the Java side in `java/lang/Class` which is lazily populated with the key being a `long` representing the ROM method pointer, and the value being the pair of method name and signature. This solution allows us to reuse such a cache in other places within the JVM, i.e. `getStackTrace` API.
- Option 4: Rather than using a cache, attempt to recover some of the performance by improving the hashing functions, and the string comparison functions. Perhaps caching the hash of the UTF8 string on the RAM/ROM method could save cycles as well.
- Option 5: Other suggestions?

issue_title: SCC directory of nonpersistent cache on a shared drive is problematic
description:
When JVM creates a non-persistent SCC, there are 4 artifacts:
1. A SysV shared memory. 2. A SysV semaphore. 3. A control file for the shared memory. 4. A control file for the semaphore.
The relationship between the SysV object vs its control file is 1 vs 1. The control files (3 and 4) are in the cache directory. However, if the cache directory is on a shared drive (across multiple machines/LPARs), the 1 vs 1 relationship can be broken. (Control file is shared across machines, SysV objects are not)
As the information in the control file can be correct only for one SysV object on one machine, JVMs on other machines could see various kinds of failures, e.g. memory/semaphore id mismatch, traceasssert or corruptcache failures. Also when the control file is destroyed, SysV objects on other machines are leaked. The default cache directory of OpenJ9 is user's home. We have user setting home on a shared drive on z/OS and seeing above failures. This issue is not limited to z/OS, but it is more frequently seen on z/OS as non-persistent cache is the default there.

issue_title: Provide output for stats bytes allocated in the heap per Java thread
description:
There is the new feature development request. This issue is created to discuss optimum shape of this feature as well as an implementation details.
Amend the verboseGC output so that there is an option to provide details of how much memory a thread is using
Use case: this can be used to identify which JVM threads are using the most memory
Administrators can correlate this with JVM logs to investigate how to reduce the memory usage
The current GC output only provides details for the thread that is using the most memory.
This doesn't help if you are trying to understand which threads are using the most memory (and you don't have access to a heapdump generated at that time)
Having this information is VERY useful if you are trying to understand the memory usage and which threads are using the memory.
Maximo threads can use a lot of memory and it isn't always possible to identify which ones use the memory.
If you can identify the threads that have the most memory then you can investigate the related user operations and discuss ways to reduce the memory usage
Currently each JVM attached thread accumulates Thread Local Heap (TLH) / non-TLH bytes allocated in the object heap between Stop-The-World (STW) Garbage Collections events. At the beginning of STW Garbage Collection all Java threads should be walked for flushing of the TLH caches. An allocation stats for each thread are reviewed at the same time (currently to get maximum-per-thread allocated) and cleared as well. So requested data exists already.
However there are two concerns regarding providing output in VerboseGC log:
- The number of threads might be really large (thousands) and unconditional output of allocation stats for each thread before every STW GC event is going to pollute log file a lot and increase it's size dramatically. Also it would cause significant negative performance impact.
- Considering how code is organized it might be hard to provide direct output to VerboseGC log at the time caches are flushed. So most likely we are going to need to create temporary data structure for information consolidation. Again, with large number of threads It might be a reason for footprint increase.
I believe an alternative solution might be using tracepoints activated on demand (and be redirected as desired). This is lightest and easiest solution.

issue_title: Create an MBean to provide access to the last recorded thread/memory usage
description:
There is the new feature development request. This issue is created to discuss optimum shape of this feature as well as an implementation details.
Create an MBean to provide access to the last recorded thread/memory usage as calculated by the last GC run
Needs to provide to list of threads:
* threadId
* thread name
* memory usage in bytes
* memory usage as % of heap
* date/time that the figures were taken
If a GC policy splits them memory into different areas then it would be useful if it provided the memory usage figure/% for each area e.g. nursery
this can be used to immediately initiate diagnostic action to gather details about the JVM threads that are using the most memory.
Code can use this information to gather more details about the thread that is using a lot of memory.
There are times when a thread almost exhausts the available memory and forces lots of GC pauses. If the thread does not trigger an out of memory exception then system administrators have very little information about which thread caused the problem.
The current GC output in the native_stderr.log file only provides details for the thread that is using the most memory.
This doesn't help if you are trying to understand which threads are using the most memory (and you don't have access to a heapdump generated at that time). There could be multiple threads that are using a lot of memory.
If a thread was running in the JVM and identified a thread that was using a lot of memory then it could take any of these actions:
- Analyse the stack trace to identify the type of activity that is occurring
-- In the Maximo world we want users to perform certain integration related activities on a particular cluster of JVMs to avoid a JVM running out of memory. The stack trace can indicate the type of operation
- Write a log message to indicate which thread was using a lot of memory
- Write a log message to indicate when the memory has been released
- Initiate further application level diagnostics e.g. enabling particular application level loggers to gather more detail
- Generate heapdump/javacore to capture details of the objects in memory
A developer may use it in this case:
- Check if a thread performing a particular operation is using a lot of memory e.g. a new piece of code or when trying to identify which of several processes is causing a leak
the log entries can be cross referenced against other entries to determine what the user was doing/identify which components may have been triggered
The memory usage figures could be from the last GC collection an stored in a Java object.
Currently there is no information available so even slightly old information would be better than nothing. The API documentation could explain how/when the information is gathered.
This item has logical relation to (the same data source)
@DanHeidinga @pshipton Do you know examples of similar implementations? It would be significantly more effective to implement commonly used API then develop proprietary mechanism.

issue_title: Improve error message when loading an invalid class version
description:
Current, if we try to run a more recent Java class in an old JVM, we get the following error message:
Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class some.Class
 java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: JVMCFRE003 bad major version; class=some/Class, offset=6
However, it is not so easily to detect that the class was compiled with a version above the supported by the JVM.Hotspot gives a more informative error message, so maybe it would be possible to improve the message in some way. Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class some.Class
 java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: some/Class has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 61.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 60.0

issue_title: ValueTypes: Add acmpne jit runtime helper
description:
Currently the JIT uses the jitAcmpHelper to perform object equality and inequality comparisons. For symmetry we are adding a `jitAcmpNEHelper` to test for inequality. This would avoid the JIT having to either negate the result of jitAcmpHelper or invert the sense of any test of the result of the call.
The reason for this deals with oddities about the way the JIT assigns profiling frequencies to different blocks in the IL.
This work is mostly boiler plate. We will need the following targets in cnathelp
- `old_fast_jitAcmpneHelper`
- "fast_jitAcmpneHelper`
These can essentially copy the existing implementation of `jitAcmpHelper` and negate the result of `valueTypeCapableAcmp`
Also rename existing `jitAcmpHelper` to `jitAcmpeqHelper`

issue_title: Enhance javacore output to indicate which options where ignored
description:
There are a lot of hotspot args that J9 ignores. These show up in the javacore output. ie.
2CIUSERARG -Xloggc:verbosegc.txt
2CIUSERARG -XX:AdaptiveSizePolicyWeight=90
2CIUSERARG -XX:CICompilerCount=2
2CIUSERARG -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
2CIUSERARG -XX:GCTimeRatio=4
2CIUSERARG -XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=20
2CIUSERARG -XX:MinHeapFreeRatio=10
2CIUSERARG -XX:ParallelGCThreads=8
2CIUSERARG -XX:+UseParallelOldGC
2CIUSERARG -XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize=528482304
2CIUSERARG -XX:InitialHeapSize=2147483648
2CIUSERARG -XX:MaxHeapSize=5368709120
2CIUSERARG -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=536870912
2CIUSERARG -XX:+PrintGC
2CIUSERARG -XX:+PrintGCTimeStamps
2CIUSERARG -XX:+UseCompressedClassPointers
2CIUSERARG -XX:+UseCompressedOop
It will be helpful for service engineers and anyone debugging using a javacore to be able to quickly identify which options the JVM ignored.

issue_title: Performance overhead for java.util.ref.Reference.refersTo() in Java 17+
description:
Java 16 introduced a new `java.util.ref.Reference.refersTo` method. This method is being used in methods in `java.lang.ThreadLocal$ThreadLocalMap`. In previous versions of Java, `ThreadLocalMap` used the `Reference.get` method.
It looks like these uses of [`refersTo`]( have introduced some overhead for uses of `ThreadLocalMap`. I'm seeing a large bump in calls to `internalEnterVMForJNI` and `internalExitVMForJNI`. I'm just crafting a stand-alone test that demonstrates that, but @keithc-ca asked me to open an issue in the meanwhile.

issue_title: Improve implementation of Reference.refersTo()
description:
The current implementations (both regular and FAST_JNI) of `java.lang.ref.Reference.refersTo()` use `j9gc_objaccess_referenceGet()` which delegates to `referenceGet()` for the relevant GC barrier.
In the case of `MM_RealtimeAccessBarrier`, this ensures the referent is marked which may alter its reachability (needlessly).
Ideally, this could be simplified to a use of `J9VMJAVALANGREFREFERENCE_REFERENT_VM()` for comparison with the given target object reference.
If appropriate, this change should apply to both the regular and FAST_JNI implementations and to code generated by the JIT compiler.

issue_title: Valhalla Class.isValueType() implementation is required
description:
> java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: jdk/internal/reflect/GeneratedMethodAccessor3
This NCDF was due to a verification failure `staticverify.c:j9bcv_verifyClassStructure` --> `chverify.c:bcvCheckClassName/checkNameImpl` at The `info->bytes` (`Ljava/lang/String;`) is a `Class` ended with `;` but not an array or `valuetypes` hence `-1` is returned.
Current `Class.descriptorString()` only appends `Q` for `PrimitiveClass` This `Class.descriptorString()` is invoked by `valhalla/lworld:MethodAccessorGenerator.java` [1] via `AccessorGenerator.java :getClassName(c, true))` [2].
JDK18 head stream `jdk/openj9:MethodAccessorGenerator.java` [2] calls `getClassName(c, false)` which doesn't invoke `Class.descriptorString()`, that's why JDK18 head stream works w/ `--enable-inline-types`.
A quick experiment shows changing back to `getClassName(c, false)` can workaround this `NoClassDefFoundError`.
Maybe an actual implementation for `Class.isValueType()` is required?
[1] [2] [3] _Originally posted by @JasonFengJ9 in

issue_title: JVMTI VMStart callback is not called?
description:
We started experiencing strange exceptions or even JVM crashes while testing the OpenJ9 Java 17 milestone 2 with YourKit Java Profiler agent (we're working on adding official support of OpenJ9 Java 17).
The JVM is:
openjdk version "17" 2021-09-14
IBM Semeru Runtime Open Edition 17.0.0.0-m1 (build 17+35)
Eclipse OpenJ9 VM 17.0.0.0-m1 (build openj9-0.28.0-m2, JRE 17 Windows 10 amd64-64-Bit Compressed References 20210916_31 (JIT enabled, AOT enabled)
OpenJ9 - 12ac773fe
OMR - 377314cb0
JCL - 41171df43e2 based on jdk-17+35)
)
When tracing starts, java.lang.UnsatisfiedLinkError with message like "attempt to recursively bind a native method" for the profiler callbacks is thrown. There is no problem with older OpenJ9 versions (Java 8, java 11, Java 16) with the same agent and options.
As we discovered from the agent logs, the problem happens likely due to the fact that VMStart is not called, and the call to jni->RegisterNatives(...) which the agent performs in VMStart does not run.

Summary of problem
We use a proprietary native agent which takes stack samples using AsyncGetCallTrace() API, from the context of a signal handler. This works reliably in HotSpot VM (in the sense that the JVM is stable, AsyncGetCallTrace has its known sampling problems).
When used with a recent-enough OpenJ9 VM, which supports AGCT, the VM either hangs or crashes, typically with an OutOfMemoryError message. The crash doesn't happen with our agent in the stack trace, but it happens only if the AGCT functionality is being used. Hopefully something can be learned from the crash dumps.
Perhaps it's useful to mention that we use per-thread timers to invoke the signal, that is each thread is receiving a signal when its CPU time has crossed a threshold, and that means we can be executing AGCT in more than one thread by more than one core in parallel.

issue_title: j9constantpool doesn't check versions properly
description:
Summary of problem
`j9constantpool` [1] doesn't check versions properly for `classref`, `fieldref`, and maybe others.
JDK8 doesn't have the class `java.lang.invoke.FilterArgumentsWithCombinerHandle`
However `j9vmconstantpool.h` generated for JDK8 has following
#define J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_JAVALANGINVOKEFILTERARGUMENTSWITHCOMBINERHANDLE 80
#define J9VMJAVALANGINVOKEFILTERARGUMENTSWITHCOMBINERHANDLE(vm) J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_CLASS_AT(vm, J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_JAVALANGINVOKEFILTERARGUMENTSWITHCOMBINERHANDLE)
#define J9VMJAVALANGINVOKEFILTERARGUMENTSWITHCOMBINERHANDLE_OR_NULL(vm) (J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_CLASSREF_AT(vm, J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_JAVALANGINVOKEFILTERARGUMENTSWITHCOMBINERHANDLE)->value)
Similarly JDK8 doesn't have the field `java.lang.reflect.Field.trustedFinal`
JDK8 `j9vmconstantpool.h` still has following
#define J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_JAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL 193
#define J9VMJAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL_OFFSET(vmThread) J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_FIELD_OFFSET(J9VMTHREAD_JAVAVM(vmThread), J9VMCONSTANTPOOL_JAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL)
#define J9VMJAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL(vmThread, object) ((void)0, \
 J9OBJECT_U32_LOAD(vmThread, object, J9VMJAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL_OFFSET(vmThread)))
#define J9VMJAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_SET_TRUSTEDFINAL(vmThread, object, value) ((void)0, \
 J9OBJECT_U32_STORE(vmThread, object, J9VMJAVALANGREFLECTFIELD_TRUSTEDFINAL_OFFSET(vmThread), (value)))
This is the reason why some code not for JDK8 w/o `#if JAVA_SPEC_VERSION >= 11` still compiles.
A quick search shows there are large number of such code snippet w/o matching `JAVA_SPEC_VERSION` defines.
 Proposed solution
It can be fixed in two stages.
* First stage
 * Fix `j9constantpool` to enforce version check such that no new defines can escape the version range;
 * Remove existing version specification within `vmconstantpool.xml` that have build breakage due to the version check applied above; * Second stage
 * Restore the version specification w/ proper `JAVA_SPEC_VERSION` defines. fyi @keithc-ca @pshipton @tajila [1]

description:
StackOverflowError

We will also need to make sure that the MethodHandle API (`java.lang.invoke` package) is initialized before the reflection API is used.

issue_title: OpenJ9 supports -XX:[+|-]ShowHiddenFrames?
description:
## OpenJDK (RI) behaviours
RI has a command line option `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+ShowHiddenFrames` to hide hidden frames (by default) and show those frames when requested.
For a test code snippet using `Lambda`:
Consumer<String> con = TestNPE::testFunc;
con.accept("Hi ");
public static void testFunc(String str) {
 new Throwable("Got: " + str).printStackTrace();
}
By default, RI hides the `Lambda` frames:
java.lang.Throwable: Got: Hi at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testFunc(TestNPE.java:55)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:46)
W/ `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+ShowHiddenFrames`:
java.lang.Throwable: Got: Hi at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testFunc(TestNPE.java:55)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE$$Lambda$1/<hex>.accept(Unknown Source)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:46)
For a test code snippet using `JEP416` `MH`:
 NullPointerException.class.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance().printStackTrace();
By default, RI hides the MH frames:
java.lang.NullPointerException
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.newInstance(DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.java:67)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstanceWithCaller(Constructor.java:499)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstance(Constructor.java:483)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:25)
W/ `-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+ShowHiddenFrames`:
java.lang.NullPointerException
 at java.base/java.lang.invoke.DirectMethodHandle$Holder.newInvokeSpecial(DirectMethodHandle$Holder)
 at java.base/java.lang.invoke.Invokers$Holder.invokeExact_MT(Invokers$Holder)
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.invokeImpl(DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.java:91)
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.newInstance(DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.java:67)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstanceWithCaller(Constructor.java:499)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstance(Constructor.java:483)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:25)
## OpenJ9 behaviours
OpenJ9 output for first test case:
java.lang.Throwable: Got: Hi at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testFunc(TestNPE.java:55)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE$$Lambda$1/<hex>.accept(Unknown Source)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:46)
OpenJ9 output for second test case:
java.lang.NullPointerException
 at java.lang.invoke.LambdaForm$DMH/<hex>.newInvokeSpecial(LambdaForm$DMH)
 at java.lang.invoke.LambdaForm$MH/<hex>.invokeExact_MT(LambdaForm$MH)
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.invokeImpl(DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.java:91)
 at java.base/jdk.internal.reflect.DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.newInstance(DirectConstructorHandleAccessor.java:67)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstanceWithCaller(Constructor.java:499)
 at java.base/java.lang.reflect.Constructor.newInstance(Constructor.java:483)
 at a.se.npe.TestNPE.testAll(TestNPE.java:25)
Ideally OpenJ9 can hide those `Lambda`/`LambdaForm`MH frames by default to match RI behaviours, which also might simplify `FrameIterator` checking for `J9AccMethodFrameIteratorSkip`.

issue_title: jextract/jpackcore missing from JRE
description: While trying to assist a user of the Semeru jre we discovered that the jextract/jpackcore utility is not included in the distribution. I downloaded the latest Java11 jre and sdk from and confirmed that the utilities are there in the sdk but not in the jre. Since service relies on the user being able to run this utility to collect the full set of crash data it's a major problem to not have it in the JRE. Please consider adding it.
creator: JamesKingdon

issue_title: Deal with time changes between Snapshot and Restore environments
description:
Any mechanism that relies on elapsed time could potentially cause issues with Snapshot/Restore.
Using j.u.Timers or even System.nanoTime to compute elapsed time could be error prone with snapshot/restore as an indeterminate amount of time may elapse between snapshot and the restore environment. Also, it is possible that one may observe negative elapsed time.
1) We need to determine all the cases where this problem can arise
- java.util.Timer
- System.getCurrentTimeMillis //this may already work but will verify
- System.nanotime()//its elapsed time
- java.util.TimeZone
- java.time package
- MXBeans, time related metrics, (cpu time, runtime, etc.)
2) We need to provide workarounds (where possible) for these cases
- for j.u.Timers we can fix them up at restore time so it omits down time between checkpoint and ad restore.

issue_title: Allow users to auto-generate all test jobs
description:
Currently, users can set `AUTOMATIC_GENERATION` at the top-level job to auto-generate the first-level test jobs. The second-level test jobs (in parallel cases) will not be auto-generated. This will cause an in-sync of test jobs. For example, `USE_TESTENV_PROPERTIES ` was introduced recently. And it is only available at the first-level test jobs, but not the second-level test jobs (i.e., xxx_testList_x).
 should also set `GENERATE_JOBS` param to generate all child test jobs.
creator: llxia
text:
Bug Title: Allow users to auto-generate all test jobs
Bug Description: Currently, users can set `AUTOMATIC_GENERATION` at the top-level job to auto-generate the first-level test jobs. The second-level test jobs (in parallel cases) will not be auto-generated. This will cause an in-sync of test jobs. For example, `USE_TESTENV_PROPERTIES ` was introduced recently. And it is only available at the first-level test jobs, but not the second-level test jobs (i.e., xxx_testList_x).
 should also set `GENERATE_JOBS` param to generate all child test jobs.

For primitive class (value type in the current OpenJ9 code), both `ACC_PRIMITIVE` and `ACC_VALUE` are set.
For value class, only `ACC_VALUE` (<hex>) is set.
Currently, OpenJ9 has flag `J9AccValueType` (<hex>) for `ACC_VALUE`. New flag needs to be added to recognize `ACC_PRIMITIVE`.

For primitive class (value type in the current OpenJ9 code), both `ACC_PRIMITIVE` and `ACC_VALUE` are set.
For value class, only `ACC_VALUE` (<hex>) is set.
Currently, OpenJ9 has flag `J9AccValueType` (<hex>) for `ACC_VALUE`. New flag needs to be added to recognize `ACC_PRIMITIVE`.

issue_title: Non-tearable value classes
description:
The original ValueTypes has been split into 2 types of classes in the new model:
1. [Value Classes]( (classes with `ACC_VALUE`)
2. [Primitive Classes]( (classes with both`ACC_VALUE` and `ACC_PRIMITIVE`)
With OpenJ9 now recognizes value classes. For value classes, it requires atomic read and write, so tearing is not allowed. This means flattening can only be done for value classes <= 64 bits (currently OpenJ9 only checks `ACC_VALUE` to set `J9ClassIsFlattened`). As value classes are nullable, if we decide to flatten value classes <= 64 bits, an additional field/bit needs to be added to represent null. Also this means OpenJ9 needs to add/support a new object model. Alternatively, we could disable flattening for value classes.

issue_title: CRIU: Blocking identity operations in single thread mode
description:
When running in single thread mode certain operations may cause a deadlock. The following are the cases where deadlocks may occur.
1) Contended monitor enters
- If the JVM attempts to acquire a lock that is held by another application thread, this would cause a deadlock since in this mode only a single application thread can be active.
- In this mode the JVM will throw an exception for any contended monitor acquisition, either by bytecode (monitorEnter) or by JNI (MonitorEnter) or java.util.concurrent.locks.Locks.
- In this mode we will also throw for Thread.join()
2) Terminal operations
- Some operations force the thread to block and require another thread to enable resumption. Given that only single thread can be run at a time this would cause a deadlock
- An internal list of known methods that exhibit this behaviour will be created. Examples are sun.misc.Unsafe.park(), java.lang.Thread.suspend.
- Upon entry to these methods the JVM will throw an exception
3) Potentially terminal operations
- Some operations that rely on external resources (sockets, file handles, etc.) may exhibit terminally blocking behaviour if there is a failure in the external system. These cases are addressed by the use of the timeout thread.
- Launch timeout thread that will interupt Java hooks if it exceeds a certain threshold
4) Notify
- Notify potentially transfers control from from the calling thread to the another that is waiting on it. Under normal circumstances it would be acceptable to send notify() and release the lock, then attempt to re-acquire it at another time. However, in single thread mode this will trigger a deadlock.
- The JVM will delay all notify operations until the end of the single thread phase
5) Temporary blocking operations
- Some operations will block temporarily - Thread.onSpinWait(), yield(), this should be a no-op in single thread mode
